about: Every developer-facing diagnostic Lattice Grid prints to the console, by the key it de-duplicates on. The key is the stable identifier: it is the `id` of every reported entry `grid.diagnostics.warnings()` hands back, what the devtools panel lists, and what to quote in a support conversation. A `*` in an id stands for a value filled in at runtime (a column id, a chart id, an event name), so `icon:*` is one entry covering every column the icon renderer refuses.

fields.id: the de-duplication key, with `*` for a runtime value
fields.module: which bundle raises it: core, dom or worker are the grid itself, anything else is the optional module of that name
fields.severity: warn (console.warn) or info (console.info); every line is prefixed [lattice]
fields.since: the release whose commit last touched the call site, derived from git blame. It is the release the diagnostic was introduced in unless the line was edited later, in which case it is later than the truth; it is never earlier.
fields.message: the sentence printed, with {placeholders} for the values filled in at runtime
fields.computed: present and true when the sentence is assembled by a helper rather than written at the call site, so there is no literal template to quote
fields.meaning: what happened, and what the grid did about it
fields.snippet: the smallest configuration that fixes it, where configuration is the answer
fields.docs: the section of the API reference that covers the feature

warnings.message: ai.actorBar() needs a DOM element to mount into; none was given and there is no document.
warnings.meaning: The governed-actor bar — the propose/preview/approve strip — had no element to mount into. Nothing was mounted, so there is no way for a user to approve a proposal in the UI, though `propose()` and `applyProposal()` still work from code.
warnings.fix: Pass the element, or set `element` on the controller's config.

warnings.message: ai.askBar() needs a DOM element to mount into; none was given and there is no document.
warnings.meaning: The ask-your-data bar had nowhere to mount, for the same reasons as the insights panel: no element argument, no `config.element`, or an argument with no owner document. Nothing was mounted.
warnings.fix: Pass the element, or set `element` on the controller's config.

warnings.message: "{name}" is not an AI event; expected one of {list}.
warnings.meaning: `ai.on()` was given an event name the AI controller never emits, so the handler can never run. The subscription is still made; the typo is named.
warnings.fix: Use one of the names in the message — `narrative`, `query` or `error`.

warnings.message: attachExplain() needs a document to build a button.
warnings.meaning: `attachExplain()` builds a button element, and there is no document to build it in — neither the mount option nor `config.element` resolves to one. `null` is returned and no button exists.
warnings.fix: Pass `mount` (or set `config.element`) so the module can find the document. This call has no meaning in a headless environment.

warnings.message: ai.insights() needs a DOM element to mount into; none was given and there is no document.
warnings.meaning: The insights panel had no element to mount into: none was passed, `config.element` is unset, and what was passed has no owner document. Nothing was mounted and the controller was returned unchanged, so the panel simply is not there.
warnings.fix: Pass the element, or set `element` when you create the controller. In a headless or server environment there is nothing to mount and the panel should not be called at all.

warnings.message: the AI ask() returned no narrative text; nothing to show. Ensure your ask() resolves to a string or { text } for a narrative prompt.
warnings.meaning: The model loop finished with no text: your `ask()` resolved to something with no `text`, or to an empty string. There is nothing to reconcile and nothing to paint, so the narrative is empty. Tool calls may still have run — this is about the final answer, not the intermediate steps.
warnings.fix: Return a string, or an object with a `text` property, from `ask()`. A provider SDK usually needs its response unwrapped before it is returned.

warnings.message: createAI needs a Lattice grid instance to ground on (grid.statistics/grid.rows). Pass the grid returned by createGrid or createHeadlessGrid.
warnings.meaning: `createAI()` was called with something that is not a grid, or with a grid that exposes neither `statistics` nor `rows`. The AI layer grounds every figure it produces in numbers it reads from the grid, so without one it has nothing to ground on: the controller is still returned, but narratives and answers will have no data behind them.
warnings.fix: Pass the object returned by `createGrid` or `createHeadlessGrid` as the first argument.
warnings.snippet:
const grid = createGrid(el, config);
const ai = createAI(grid, { ask });

warnings.message: a risk summary needs a Gantt and/or a Kanban board to ground on. Pass { kind: "risk", gantt, board } (or precomputed earnedValue/schedule/breaches); there is nothing to summarise.
warnings.meaning: A risk summary was requested and none of its three sources was available: no schedule, no earned value, no SLA breaches. The summary is built from facts, and with no source there are no facts — so what comes back has nothing in it to narrate.
warnings.fix: Pass the `gantt` controller and/or the kanban `board`, or hand in pre-computed `earnedValue`, `schedule` or `breaches` objects.

warnings.message: modules/angular is deprecated: it needs the JIT compiler. Use @toclocoinc/lattice-grid/angular.
warnings.meaning: `createLatticeGrid` from `@toclocoinc/lattice-grid/modules/angular` builds its component class at run time, which only works on a page that ships Angular's JIT compiler. A production (AOT) Angular build does not ship one, so this route works in development and throws in production — which is why it is deprecated rather than merely discouraged. The warning is raised as soon as the factory is called, before the compiler is even checked.
warnings.fix: Import the ahead-of-time components from the grid package's Angular entry point instead. They are in the same install, need no compiler and work under AOT.

warnings.message: <lattice-tabs>: `tabs` changed (a label, a badge or a descriptor), but the strip takes it only when created — the module has no way to repaint an existing tab. Nothing was applied and the strip was NOT rebuilt, because rebuilding it would lose whichever tab is open and any state its content holds. Put the strip inside an `@if` keyed on what changed if a genuine rebuild is wanted; a live badge otherwise belongs in your own template.
warnings.meaning: `ngOnChanges` on the Angular tabs component saw a new `tabs` array. The strip reads its descriptors once at construction and has no method to repaint one, so the change could not be applied; the component reports it rather than rebuilding, which would close the open tab.
warnings.fix: Wrap the element in an `@if` you toggle when a new strip is genuinely wanted. Keep a live badge in your own template.

warnings.message: a rolling time window needs a continuous x axis; this chart bands its x values, so the window is ignored. Bind a date or numeric column to x.
warnings.meaning: A rolling time window was configured on a chart whose x axis is banded — either the bound dimension is categorical, or the type is a bar, which always sits in a band whatever its dimension's type. A band has no domain to roll, so the window was ignored and every category is drawn.
warnings.fix: Bind a date or numeric column to `x` and use a type that scales it (line, area, scatter, step), or drop the window.

warnings.message: axis window kind "{kind}" is not supported on a chart axis; only { kind: "time", span } rolls the domain. Bound the row count with the source's maxRows instead.
warnings.meaning: An `axis.x.window` was configured with a `kind` other than `'time'`. A chart axis can roll only over time — a count-based window is a property of the data, not of the drawing — so the window was ignored entirely and the axis covers the whole domain.
warnings.fix: Use `{ kind: 'time', span }` to roll the axis, or cap the rows at the source with `maxRows` if you wanted the last N readings.
warnings.snippet: createChart({ grid, container, axis: { x: { window: { kind: 'time', span: 300000 } } } });

warnings.message: chart bound nothing from the {n} row(s) the grid is showing, so it shows its empty state. The binding named no series to draw: check that the spec names the columns this chart needs — a flow type needs source and target, a measure needs a column with values in it.
warnings.meaning: The grid has rows and the binding produced nothing from them, so the chart shows its empty state over data that is plainly there. The other empty case — a grid with no rows at all — is deliberately *not* reported: the viewer can see it, there is nothing for an integrator to do, and a dashboard that starts empty must not print a line per chart on its way to drawing.
warnings.fix: Check that the spec names the columns this chart type needs. A flow type needs `source` and `target`; a measure needs a column that actually holds values.

warnings.message: a candlestick chart needs four measures — open, high, low and close, in that order — and only {n} were bound. Pass them as measures: [open, high, low, close].
warnings.meaning: A type whose required inputs are not all present. A candlestick needs four measures in a fixed order; given fewer it drew nothing at all, and a chart that silently draws nothing is indistinguishable from a broken one, so the picture is refused and the empty state shown.
warnings.fix: Pass all four measures, in order.
warnings.snippet: createChart({ grid, container, type: 'candlestick', x: 'date', measures: ['open', 'high', 'low', 'close'] });

warnings.message: chart {key}: "{col}" names a column this grid does not have, so there is nothing to read and nothing to draw. The columns it does have: … Bind a column the grid declares, or declare the column.
warnings.meaning: A column named in the chart spec is not a column of the grid. It is asked first, before emptiness, because a missing column does not produce an empty binding: every row answers `undefined` for it, which is one category or one null measure, so a chart bound to one would otherwise draw a complete frame around nothing. The chart shows its empty state instead, and the message lists the columns the grid does have.
warnings.fix: Bind a column the grid declares — the id, not the header title — or declare the column on the grid. The spec key that named it (`x`, `y`, `measures`, `source`, `target`, …) is printed with it.
warnings.snippet: createChart({ grid, container, type: 'bar', x: 'region', y: 'amount' });

warnings.message: chart x column "{col}" is drawn on a {time|continuous} axis, and not one of its {n} value(s) reads as a {date|number} — so the axis would be drawn over a domain invented from nothing rather than measured from the data. Remove axis.x.scale to let the column choose its own scale, or type the column so its values parse.
warnings.meaning: A continuous x axis was asked for and the values yield no extent, so every coordinate on the axis would be invented: a text column pinned to `scale: 'linear'` drew a line against an axis labelled 0.0 to 1.0, and pinned to `'time'`, against two ticks at the epoch. There is no honest picture, so none is drawn. A *zero-width* extent is different and still draws — one reading padded to an interval around itself is the truthful picture of one reading.
warnings.fix: Remove `axis.x.scale` and let the column choose its own scale, or type the column so its values parse as dates or numbers.

warnings.message: chart "x" expects one column id (a string) and was given an array [{ids}]. A chart takes one category column on "x". For a hierarchy, group the grid — grid.columns.group([...]) — and the hierarchical types (pie, donut, sunburst, treemap) read the grouping.
warnings.meaning: `x` was an array. It is the shape a reader guesses for "nest by these two", and the chart has no such reading: the array reaches the grid's column lookup, which takes one id, so nothing resolves and the chart draws empty. The diagnostic is raised per chart and before the binding, so it precedes whatever the binding then makes of it.
warnings.fix: Give `x` one column id. For a hierarchy, group the grid and use a hierarchical type, which reads the grouping rather than a list of columns.

warnings.message: {n} reading(s) on the x axis{ column} were not drawn: stamped up to {lead} ahead of this device's clock, which is more than the {limit} ({share} of the {span} rolling window) a reading may run ahead and still move the window. This is a producer whose clock is wrong, not a window that is too narrow
warnings.meaning: Readings arrived stamped further into the future than the rolling window's lead allowance. They are not drawn, and — more importantly — they are not allowed to carry the window, because a single badly fast producer would otherwise push every other producer's recent readings out of view. A chart whose only producer is fast therefore shows its empty state, and this line is why.
warnings.fix: Fix the producer's clock, or stamp readings with a server time rather than a device time. Widening `axis.x.window.span` will not help: the readings are ahead of the window, not behind it.

warnings.message: the rolling x window covers the last {span} ms, and the newest of {n} x value(s) is {age}s old, so every mark would be drawn outside the plot. The chart shows its empty state instead. Seed it with data inside the window, widen axis.x.window.span, or drop the window while showing history.
warnings.meaning: A rolling window that no longer reaches the data. Every mark would be drawn far outside the plot, with the axes, the legend and the accessible table all rendering normally, so the chart reads as broken while nothing is wrong with the data. It is asked before anything is dropped, so the readings it counts are exactly the ones the window removes. The key carries the column as well as the chart, so two windows over two columns are two diagnostics.
warnings.fix: Seed the chart with data inside the window, widen `axis.x.window.span`, or drop the window when showing history. If the message says the readings are stamped *ahead* of the window instead, the producer's clock is wrong — see `chart:*:x:window:ahead`.

warnings.message: chart annotation{ (label)} of kind "{kind}", reading the {axis} axis, was not drawn: {reason}.
warnings.meaning: An annotation could not be placed, so it was not drawn at all. The key carries the kind, the axis and the reason, so a band that has no second value and a line whose value is off the domain are two separate lines. Being told is the point: "drawn off-screen" and "never drawn" look identical on the canvas.
warnings.fix: The reason is printed at the end of the message — usually a missing or unreadable value, or an axis the chart does not have. Annotations that read the right axis are drawn; check `axis: 'right'` against a chart that really has a right axis.

warnings.message: geometry pack "{name}" has not been loaded, so the map fell back to the schematic continents. Import the pack module and pass it as `shapes`
warnings.meaning: A map named a geometry pack by name and no pack of that name has been loaded. Rather than quietly drawing a different map, the chart says so and falls back to the schematic continents. The message lists the packs that *are* loaded, when there are any.
warnings.fix: Import the pack module and pass the pack itself as `shapes` — the packs are separate modules so that a map of one country does not ship the whole world.
warnings.snippet:
import { pack } from '@toclocoinc/lattice-grid/modules/geo-uk';
createChart({ grid, container, type: 'geomap', shapes: pack });

warnings.message: (the projection resolver's own explanation of why the named projection could not be used)
warnings.meaning: The projection named on a map (or carried by its geometry pack) could not be resolved or configured, so the map was drawn with the resolver's fallback. The text comes from the projection resolver itself and names the projection and the reason.
warnings.fix: Use one of the projections the charts module documents, and check the `projectionOptions` that go with it — a projection given parameters it does not take is the usual cause.

warnings.message: Unknown icon '{name}' on a network node; drew a plain disc instead. Register it with registerIcon or config.icons, or name a built-in.
warnings.meaning: The grid has an icon registry and it holds no icon under that name. The node drew as a plain disc, so the chart is complete but unlabelled by icon.
warnings.fix: Register the icon before the chart draws, or use one of the built-in names.

warnings.message: A network node asked for the icon '{name}', but this grid publishes no icon registry — a headless grid has no sprites. The node drew as a plain disc.
warnings.meaning: A network chart node named an icon and the grid it is bound to has no icon registry at all, which is what a headless grid looks like — the sprites live in the DOM layer. The node is still drawn, as a plain disc.
warnings.fix: Bind the chart to a grid created with `createGrid` (which publishes the registry), or drop the icon names from the node specs.

warnings.message: chart measure fn {fn} is not a known aggregation; using '{default}'. Supported: {list}.
warnings.meaning: A measure named an aggregation that does not exist. The chart falls back to the default aggregation and still draws — which is exactly the danger, because a chart drawn from a mistyped `fn` looks plausible and is wrong. That is why it is named, with the value and the supported set, rather than left to be discovered.
warnings.fix: Use one of the aggregations listed in the message.

warnings.message: chart x column "{col}" is typed "{type}", so its {n} values are drawn as categories on a band scale even though they all read as {dates|numbers}. Type the column {'date'|'number'} for a continuous axis, or pin it with axis: { x: { scale: '{kind}' } }.
warnings.meaning: The x column is typed `text` (or is untyped, which an inference over an empty row set produces), and every one of its values reads as a date or a number. The chart drew them as categories — evenly spaced bands in row order — which looks like a time series with the gaps removed. Only `text`/untyped columns are reported: a `lookup` whose codes are integers, or a boolean drawn as two bands, is the caller stating what the column holds, and telling them it looks continuous would be noise.
warnings.fix: Type the column so the inference is not needed, or pin the axis with `axis.x.scale`.

warnings.message: chart x column "{col}" is a 'date', which stores a calendar day, so all {n} rows collapsed into one point and were reduced by '{fn}'. For a series inside a single day, type the column 'datetime' or bind epoch milliseconds.
warnings.meaning: A `date` column stores `YYYY-MM-DD`, so sub-day timestamps arrive as copies of one day and the reduction runs over the lot: one point whose value totals things that were never meant to be totalled. The resolution is gone before the chart sees it. For a type that scales its x there is no series left to draw and the picture is refused; a *bar* of one day's total is an honest reduction and still draws. The binder notices the collapse and the drawability pass decides the picture — both report under this one key, so an integrator reads one line.
warnings.fix: Type the column `'datetime'` (or `'timestamp'`), or bind epoch milliseconds, so the readings keep their time of day.

warnings.message: chart axis.x.scale "{scale}" is not a scale this chart draws. Use one of: {list}. The scale was chosen from the column instead.
warnings.meaning: `axis.x.scale` named a scale the chart has no implementation for. It was ignored rather than guessed at, and the scale was chosen from the column's type as it would have been with no `scale` at all — so the chart still draws, possibly not on the axis you wanted.
warnings.fix: Use one of the names listed in the message, or remove `axis.x.scale` and type the column instead.

warnings.message: '{key}' is not a configuration key this grid recognises, so it had no effect on {column|column group} "{name}". Check the spelling against the reference.
warnings.meaning: A column or column-group definition carries a key the model does not read. It is ignored — nothing is renamed or guessed — so whatever it was meant to configure is simply not configured. The key is reported once per unknown *key*, not once per column, so forty columns carrying the same typo produce one line.
warnings.fix: Check the spelling against the column reference. The key is dropped entirely, so a mis-spelt `width` leaves the column at its default width rather than at the value you wrote.

warnings.message: column "{colId}" has no `field` and no `value.apply`, so an edit cannot be written back.
warnings.meaning: An edit was committed on a column that has nowhere to put the new value: it is not backed by a row field, and it defines no `value.apply` to write one. The edit is refused and the cell keeps its old value.
warnings.fix: Give the column a `field`, or a `value.apply` that writes the edit into the row.
warnings.snippet: columns: [{ id: 'full', value: { get: (p) => …, apply: ({ value, data }) => { data.first = value.split(' ')[0]; } } }]

warnings.message: a '{type}' before-handler rejected; the action was cancelled.
warnings.meaning: An asynchronous before-handler returned a promise that rejected. The grid waits for every deferred handler — a logging handler runs alongside a vetoing one — and treats a rejection exactly as it treats a throw: the action is cancelled and the reason reported.
warnings.fix: The rejection reason is attached to the console line. Resolve `false` to veto; resolve anything else to allow.

warnings.message: a '{type}' before-handler threw; the action was cancelled.
warnings.meaning: A before-event handler threw. A before-handler decides whether the action happens, so a throw is taken as a veto: the sort, edit, filter or move was cancelled and the corresponding `…:cancelled` event fired. It is surfaced rather than swallowed because the action is unsafe and the host has to see why.
warnings.fix: The error is attached to the console line. To veto deliberately, return `false` or call `preventDefault()`.

warnings.message: {on|once}('{type}') needs a function; ignored.
warnings.meaning: `on()` or `once()` was called with something that is not a function, so nothing was subscribed. A no-op unsubscribe function is returned, so calling code is safe.
warnings.fix: Pass the handler function itself, not its result — `grid.on('sort:changed', handler)` rather than `handler()`.

warnings.message: a '{type}' handler threw; other handlers were unaffected.
warnings.meaning: One of your event handlers threw. Delivery is isolated per handler, so every other subscriber to that event still ran and the grid carried on. The key carries the subscription name and an identity for the handler, so a handler throwing on every scroll event produces one line rather than thousands.
warnings.fix: The error is attached to the console line, with its stack.

warnings.message: {on|once}('{type}') subscribes to an event the grid never raises, so the handler will never fire. Check the name against the EventName list — a common cause is a near miss such as 'row:click' for 'row:clicked'.
warnings.meaning: The event name is not one the grid emits, so the subscription is dead: it is registered, it costs nothing, and it will never be called. The check runs in development builds only.
warnings.fix: Check the name against the events reference. Near misses — a missing `:ed`, a singular for a plural — are the usual cause.

warnings.message: rows.apply needs a rowKey to identify rows; without one, updates and removals cannot be matched.
warnings.meaning: A keyed diff names the rows it changes, and this grid identifies rows by index because no `rowKey` was declared. There is no way to match an update or a removal to a row, so those parts of the change cannot be applied.
warnings.fix: Declare `rowKey` — the field that identifies a row, or a function returning it. Keyed identity is what the live-update, diff, selection-stability and comment features all need.

warnings.message: the clipboard could not be read; handle the paste event and pass event.clipboardData instead
warnings.meaning: The asynchronous clipboard read is unavailable or was denied — no `navigator.clipboard`, an insecure context, or the user refused permission. `null` is returned and nothing is pasted.
warnings.fix: Read the clipboard from a real `paste` event, where the data is available without permission, and hand the text to the grid.

warnings.message: column '{id}' names the editor '{editor}' but does not enable editing, so it stays read-only. Add `enabled: true`, or use `edit: true` and set `editor` alongside it.
warnings.meaning: Naming an editor does not make a column editable: editing is opt-in and stays so, because inferring it from an editor name would turn one line of `columnDefaults` into "every column is editable". The editor is accepted and does nothing, and the column stays read-only — which looks exactly like a broken editor.
warnings.fix: Add `enabled: true` to the column's `edit` block.
warnings.snippet: columns: [{ id: 'status', edit: { enabled: true, editor: 'select' } }]

warnings.message: two columns resolve to the id '{id}', so the second is ignored. An id defaults to the column's field, so declare an explicit `id` when two columns read the same field.
warnings.meaning: Two column definitions ended up with the same id. The first is kept and the second refused, so the grid has one column where you declared two — everything the second definition configured is absent. A column's id defaults to its `field`, so this is usually two columns reading one field with different formatting.
warnings.fix: Give each column an explicit `id`.
warnings.snippet: columns: [{ id: 'amount', field: 'amount' }, { id: 'amountPct', field: 'amount', format: { style: 'percent' } }]

warnings.message: columns.fit(): the columns it does not size (resizable: false, and the grid's own checkbox, expander, group and tree columns) take {n}px of a {m}px viewport, leaving {k}px for {c} column(s) that need at least {f}px. They are set to their minimum widths and the grid scrolls
warnings.meaning: `columns.fit()` shares the viewport among the columns it is allowed to resize. The ones it may not touch already take more room than there is, so the sizeable columns are set to their minimum widths and the grid scrolls sideways instead of fitting. The key carries this grid's own identity, so one grid overflowing cannot use the warning up for every other grid on the page.
warnings.fix: Make some of the fixed columns resizable, narrow them, hide one, or accept the horizontal scroll.

warnings.message: no band "{id}" to dissolve.
warnings.meaning: `dissolveGroup()` named a band that does not exist, so no children were promoted and the tree is unchanged.
warnings.fix: Check the band id. A nested band dissolves into its parent band, not to the root, so the id to pass is the inner one.

warnings.message: groupColumns was given no known column ids; nothing was grouped.
warnings.meaning: Every id handed to `groupColumns()` is unknown to the grid, so there is nothing to put in a band and no band was created. `null` is returned.
warnings.fix: Pass ids from `grid.columns.all()`. Ids are matched exactly.

warnings.message: band id "{id}" is already in use; nothing was grouped.
warnings.meaning: The id chosen for a new band is already taken, by another band or by a column. The collision is checked before any column is detached, so the tree is untouched and nothing was grouped.
warnings.fix: Choose a free id, or pass `groupId` to add to the existing band instead of creating one.

warnings.message: column "{id}" is position-locked and cannot be grouped.
warnings.meaning: Putting a column into a band moves it next to the band's other columns, and this column declares `layout.lockPosition`. The whole call is refused — nothing is grouped, not even the other columns in the list — so the tree is left exactly as it was rather than half-changed.
warnings.fix: Leave the locked column out of the list, or clear its `lockPosition`.

warnings.message: no band "{id}" to move.
warnings.meaning: `moveGroup()` named a band that does not exist, so nothing moved. A band moves only among its own siblings, so the call would not have left its level in any case.
warnings.fix: Check the band id against the resolved column groups.

warnings.message: no band "{id}" to rename.
warnings.meaning: `renameGroup()` named a band that does not exist. Nothing was renamed and no change event fired.
warnings.fix: Check the band id against the resolved column groups.

warnings.message: no band "{id}" to add to; nothing was grouped.
warnings.meaning: `groupColumns(ids, { groupId })` adds columns to an existing band, and no band has that id. Nothing was grouped and no band was created — the `groupId` option never creates one.
warnings.fix: Use the `id` option to create a band with a chosen id, or pass the id of a band that exists.

warnings.message: no column "{id}" to ungroup.
warnings.meaning: `ungroupColumn()` named a column the grid does not have, so nothing was promoted and the band structure is unchanged. A column that is already at the root is not an error and says nothing.
warnings.fix: Check the id against `grid.columns.all()`.

warnings.message: comments provider is missing {methods}; those operations are unavailable.
warnings.meaning: The comments provider does not implement every method the model calls. It is still installed — the operations it does support work — and the ones named in the message do nothing when they are reached.
warnings.fix: Implement the missing methods on the provider, or leave the corresponding UI affordances switched off.

warnings.message: compareGroups needs a "by" column to split the rows into two groups.
warnings.meaning: `compareGroups` compares one measure across two groups of rows, and the `by` column is what splits them. Without it there is nothing to compare and the call returns `null`.
warnings.fix: Name the grouping column in `by`.

warnings.message: compareGroups: the chosen test had too little to work with (too few values, or no variation).
warnings.meaning: The test ran and could not produce a statistic: too few values in one group, or no variation at all within them (every value identical, so the variance is zero). `null` is returned rather than a p-value computed from a degenerate sample.
warnings.fix: Compare groups with more rows, or check that the measure actually varies within them.

warnings.message: compareGroups: the two groups must be two distinct, present values.
warnings.meaning: The two group keys resolved to the same value, or one of them is null. A comparison needs two different groups, so the call returns `null`.
warnings.fix: Pass two distinct values in `groups`, each of which appears in the `by` column.

warnings.message: compareGroups: one of the two groups has no rows in the current set.
warnings.meaning: Both group keys are valid, and one of them matches no row among the rows the grid is currently showing. There is nothing to test against, so the call returns `null`. A filter that excludes one arm of the comparison is the usual cause.
warnings.fix: Widen the filters, or compare two groups that are both present.

warnings.message: compareGroups: the "by" column has fewer than two distinct values to group by.
warnings.meaning: With no explicit `groups`, the two most frequent values of the `by` column are compared — and it has fewer than two distinct values in the current row set. There is nothing to compare, so the call returns `null`.
warnings.fix: Check the filters: the two groups have to be present in the rows the grid is currently showing. Name the two values explicitly in `groups` if the automatic choice is not what you want.

warnings.message: compareGroups: {test} needs a numeric column, but the column is not numeric.
warnings.meaning: A specific test was forced — Welch's t-test or Mann-Whitney — and both compare numeric distributions. The column is not numeric, so the test cannot be run and the call returns `null` rather than coercing values into numbers.
warnings.fix: Drop the `test` override and let the column family choose (a categorical column gets a chi-square), or compare a numeric column.

warnings.message: rows were declared twice — as the top-level `rows` option and inside the `source` block — so the top-level rows were used and the {n} row(s) in `source.rows` were ignored. Declare them once.
warnings.meaning: Two answers to one question. The top-level `rows` wins, because it is the shape every example uses and the one `rows.load()` writes to — leaving the source block's rows in place would make a later `set('rows', …)` disagree with the grid. Picking one in silence is how a host ends up debugging the rows they can see rather than the ones they declared.
warnings.fix: Declare the rows once: at the top level, or inside `source`, not both.

warnings.message: '{key}' is not a configuration key this grid recognises, so it had no effect. Check the spelling against the reference.
warnings.meaning: A top-level configuration key is not one the grid reads. It is ignored entirely — nothing is guessed — so whatever it was meant to switch on is off. Reported once per key name.
warnings.fix: Check the spelling against the configuration reference. A key that belongs on a column, or inside `source`, is a common cause.

warnings.message: '{key}' was given {value}, which is not one of the shapes it accepts. Check the type against the reference.
warnings.meaning: A configuration key was recognised and its value is not a shape it can take — the wrong primitive type, a value outside the allowed set, or something no documented shape could be. The key is ignored and the grid uses its default, so the feature behaves as though you had not configured it. The message states which of the three checks failed and, for an enumerated key, lists the values it accepts.
warnings.fix: Check the key's type in the configuration reference.

warnings.message: column "{id}" is bitset-backed with no declared row count; assuming {n}
warnings.meaning: A bitset column packs eight rows per byte, so its length cannot be recovered from the buffer: the last byte may be up to seven rows of padding. With no declared count the kernel assumes the buffer is full, which can overstate the row count by up to seven.
warnings.fix: Declare the row count on the handle (`length`, or a `presence` set) when you build a bitset column yourself.

warnings.message: the date pattern "{pattern}" contains '{ch}', which is not a supported token, so it is rendered as text. Quote it as a literal to silence this. Supported: {tokens}.
warnings.meaning: A letter in a date pattern is not one of the tokens the formatter implements — `zzz` for a zone, `QQ` for a quarter — so it is emitted as literal text and the letters themselves appear in the cell. Punctuation and spaces are legitimately literal and say nothing.
warnings.fix: Use one of the supported tokens, or quote the letters as a literal if they are meant to be text.

warnings.message: defaults() expects a configuration object, or null to clear it, but got {type}. The call was ignored and the defaults are unchanged.
warnings.meaning: `defaults()` sets the house configuration every later grid inherits. The argument was not an object, so nothing was set and whatever defaults were already in force stay in force — which is worth saying, because the symptom is a grid that quietly does not pick up your house style.
warnings.fix: Pass a configuration object, or `null` to clear the defaults.

warnings.message: computed column "{colId}" declares no `value.deps`; treating it as `deps: '*'` (a whole-row dependency). Declare the dependencies to get precise invalidation.
warnings.meaning: A computed column did not say which fields it reads, so the grid has to assume it reads all of them. The column is correct — it simply recomputes whenever anything in the row changes, instead of only when its inputs do, which costs work on every edit and every incoming delta.
warnings.fix: List the fields the getter reads in `value.deps`, or declare `deps: '*'` explicitly if it really does read the whole row.
warnings.snippet: columns: [{ id: 'net', value: { deps: ['gross', 'tax'], get: (p) => p.data.gross - p.data.tax } }]

warnings.message: detail is enabled but neither `rows` nor `render` was supplied; expanding a master would show an empty region, so it stays off.
warnings.meaning: A detail region needs something to put in it: either `rows` (a nested grid) or `render` (your own content). With neither, expanding a row would open an empty panel, which reads as a defect rather than as a missing option — so the feature is switched off instead and rows do not expand at all.
warnings.fix: Supply `detail.rows` for a nested grid, or `detail.render` to draw the panel yourself.

warnings.message: the comparator for column '{colId}' threw while diffing; the two values were compared by identity instead.
warnings.meaning: The column's comparator threw while the diff was deciding whether a value changed. The diff falls back to identity, so values that the comparator would have treated as equal — two dates a millisecond apart, two objects with the same contents — are now reported as changes.
warnings.fix: The error is attached to the console line. A comparator is called with the before and after values, either of which may be `null` or `undefined`.

warnings.message: the diff `keyOf` threw; the row was skipped.
warnings.meaning: The diff's key function threw for a row, so that row has no identity and is left out of the comparison entirely — it is neither an addition, a change nor a removal.
warnings.fix: The error is attached to the console line. `keyOf` must tolerate every row in the snapshot, including ones that predate a schema change.

warnings.message: the diff was asked about the whole data set but has no current rows: pass them in, or supply `currentRows` when constructing the DiffModel.
warnings.meaning: A whole-set question — how many rows changed, which rows are new — needs the current rows, and the model has neither an argument nor a `currentRows` supplier. The question cannot be answered and the caller gets nothing.
warnings.fix: Pass the rows to the call, or give the `DiffModel` a `currentRows` function when you construct it.

warnings.message: the diff comparator override threw; the column comparator was used instead.
warnings.meaning: The diff-level comparator override threw for a column. The column's own comparator is used instead, so the diff still works, with the default comparison rather than yours.
warnings.fix: The error is attached to the console line. An override may return `undefined` to defer to the column comparator, which is the supported way to handle only some columns.

warnings.message: reading column '{colId}' threw while diffing.
warnings.meaning: A computed column's getter threw while the diff was reading the previous or current value. That value reads as `undefined`, so the column is diffed against nothing and will usually appear as a change.
warnings.fix: The error is attached to the console line. The diff reads the *snapshot* row as well as the live one, and a snapshot may lack fields the live row has.

warnings.message: {n} snapshot row(s) produced no key and were dropped from the diff; `keyOf` must be the grid's own `rowKey`.
warnings.meaning: Rows in the snapshot produced a null or undefined key, so they could not be indexed and were dropped. The diff therefore reports every one of them as an addition on the current side, or as nothing at all — it is comparing against an incomplete past.
warnings.fix: Use the same key function as the grid's `rowKey`, so that the snapshot and the live rows agree on identity.

warnings.message: value.apply threw for column '{colId}'; the edit was discarded.
warnings.meaning: The column's `value.apply` — the hook that writes an edited value back into the row — threw. The edit is discarded and the cell keeps its old value, because a half-applied write is worse than none.
warnings.fix: The error is attached to the console line.

warnings.message: edit.confirm "manual" needs an edit.commit hook to send the write; optimistic tracking is off.
warnings.meaning: `confirm: 'manual'` means the grid holds an edit as pending until your code confirms it, which requires a `commit` hook to send the write in the first place. Without one there is nothing to confirm, so optimistic tracking is switched off entirely and edits are applied directly.
warnings.fix: Supply `edit.commit`, or drop `confirm: 'manual'`.

warnings.message: edit.confirm '{value}' is not a mode; use 'auto' or 'manual'. Treated as 'auto'.
warnings.meaning: The confirmation mode is not one of the two. It is treated as `'auto'`, so an edit is confirmed as soon as the commit hook resolves rather than waiting for your code to confirm it.
warnings.fix: Use `'auto'` or `'manual'`.

warnings.message: edit.enabled threw for column '{colId}'; the cell was treated as read-only.
warnings.meaning: The per-cell `edit.enabled` predicate threw. The cell is treated as read-only — the closed answer, so a broken predicate cannot open a cell that should have been locked.
warnings.fix: The error is attached to the console line. The predicate is called with the cell params for every cell of the column, including ones whose row data is incomplete.

warnings.message: getValue threw for column '{colId}'.
warnings.meaning: The column's `getValue` threw while the editor was reading the current value, so the editor opens on `undefined` — an empty field where the existing value should have been.
warnings.fix: The error is attached to the console line.

warnings.message: column '{colId}' is editable but has neither a field nor value.apply, so the edit had nowhere to go.
warnings.meaning: The column accepts edits and defines no destination for them: no `field` to write, no `value.apply` to call. The edit is refused and the cell is unchanged.
warnings.fix: Give the column a `field`, or a `value.apply` that writes the value into the row.

warnings.message: value.parse threw for column '{colId}'; the raw editor output was used.
warnings.meaning: `value.parse` turns what the editor produced into what the row should hold, and it threw. The raw editor output is written instead, so the row may end up holding a string where a number or a date was expected.
warnings.fix: The error is attached to the console line. `parse` receives whatever the editor returned, which for a text editor is always a string.

warnings.message: edit: true was set over a remote source but nothing can persist the write: no edit.commit hook and the source synthesised none (a read-only adapter, or one that does not declare mutate.update). Cells would change on screen
warnings.meaning: Editing was switched on over a source that cannot save anything. Optimistic tracking is off, so edits are not queued for a confirmation that will never come — but nothing persists them either, and a cell that changes on screen and reverts on the next fetch is the worst shape this can take.
warnings.fix: Supply an `edit.commit` hook that sends the write, or use an adapter that declares `mutate: { update: true }`.

warnings.message: edit.validate threw for column '{colId}'; the edit was rejected.
warnings.meaning: The validator threw, which is treated as a failed validation: the edit is rejected with a generic message rather than being accepted unvalidated. Rejecting is the safe direction — an unvalidated write is worse than a refused one.
warnings.fix: The error is attached to the console line. A validator returns `true` to accept, or a string to reject with that message.

warnings.message: column "{id}" has `group.explode`, so rows appear under each of their values and totals double-count. Group footers should be annotated accordingly.
warnings.meaning: Exploding a multi-value lookup places each row under every one of its values, so a row with three tags appears in three groups. That is what the option is for, and the arithmetic consequence is unavoidable: every total that spans those groups counts the row more than once. Nothing is refused; the double counting is named so that a footer showing it can be labelled.
warnings.fix: Nothing, if the multiple placement is what you want — but annotate the group footers so a reader knows the totals overlap. Drop `group.explode` if you need totals that add up.

warnings.message: toExcelValue threw for column '{colId}'; the stored value was exported instead.
warnings.meaning: A data type's `toExcelValue` hook converts a value into something a spreadsheet can hold, and it threw. The stored value is written instead, so the cell exports as whatever the raw value serialises to — which may be a string where a number or a date was intended.
warnings.fix: The error is attached to the console line. The hook is called for every exported cell of the column, including empty ones.

warnings.message: download requested but this environment has no DOM; returning the data instead
warnings.meaning: Starting a download means creating an anchor and clicking it, and there is no document to do that in — a worker, a server-side render, a test runner. The file was still produced: the blob is returned to the caller instead of being saved.
warnings.fix: Take the returned data and write it yourself. In a browser, check that the export is not running inside a worker.

warnings.message: no export worker supplied; streaming on the main thread instead
warnings.meaning: The worker-based Excel export was called without a worker, so it fell back to streaming on the main thread. The file is identical; the UI is blocked while it is built, which for a large export is the whole reason the worker path exists.
warnings.fix: Pass a `worker` in the transport argument.

warnings.message: filter references unknown column "{col}"; the condition passes every row
warnings.meaning: A condition names a column that has no data handle — it is not a column of this grid, or it is not loaded. There is nothing to test, so the condition passes every row and the filter does not narrow anything.
warnings.fix: Check the column id in the condition. A saved filter restored against a different column set is the usual cause.

warnings.message: filter operator "{op}" is unknown for column "{col}"; the condition is refused rather than matching every row. Valid operators here: {list}.
warnings.meaning: The operator is not one this column's type allows. The condition is dropped from the filter set rather than passing every row — the fail-closed direction, so a bad condition never widens what the user can see. The message lists the operators the column does accept.
warnings.fix: Use one of the operators listed in the message, or change the column's type if it is the type that is wrong.

warnings.message: filter condition on column "{col}" uses op "relative" with {an unknown relative date token "…"|no relative date token}; the condition is refused rather than matching every row.
warnings.meaning: A `relative` date condition carries no token, or one the grid does not know. The condition is refused — dropped from the filter set — rather than admitted as a condition that matches everything, because a filter that silently stops narrowing shows more data than the user asked to see. The message lists the tokens that are valid.
warnings.fix: Use one of the relative tokens listed in the message.

warnings.message: filters.reapply({name}) names no registered where predicate; nothing was re-run.
warnings.meaning: `reapply(name)` re-runs a registered `where` predicate whose result may have changed although the rows have not. That name is not registered, so nothing was re-run and the rows on screen are unchanged. Reporting it is what tells a refreshed filter apart from a name that was never registered.
warnings.fix: Check the name against the registered predicates. `reapply()` with no name re-runs all of them.

warnings.message: filters.where("{name}", fn, { condition }) needs a FilterSet; the predicate is registered but nothing is pushed to the source.
warnings.meaning: `condition` is the declarative twin of a predicate: the grid pushes it down to the source so the server can do the narrowing, and runs the function locally as the authority. The value given is not a filter set, so only the local predicate runs — correct results, and the whole dataset comes over the wire. The registration itself is kept, because losing a permission predicate over a malformed option is the one outcome worth designing against.
warnings.fix: Pass a filter set object as `condition`, or leave it out.

warnings.message: filters.where("{name}", fn, { deps }) needs an array of column ids; the predicate is registered but re-runs on every pass instead.
warnings.meaning: `deps` names the columns a predicate reads, so the grid can skip re-running it when nothing it depends on has changed. The value given is not an array of column ids, so it is ignored: the predicate still works and still filters correctly, and it re-runs on every pass — which is exactly the saving the option was asked for.
warnings.fix: Pass an array of non-empty column id strings.

warnings.message: filters.where("{name}", fn) needs a function; the predicate was not registered. Pass null to remove a registered predicate.
warnings.meaning: The second argument was neither a function nor `null`, so nothing was registered under that name — and anything already registered under it is still in force.
warnings.fix: Pass a predicate function, or `null` to remove one.

warnings.message: filters.where(name, fn) needs a non-empty string name; the predicate was not registered.
warnings.meaning: A `where` predicate is registered under a name so that it can be replaced, re-run or removed later. The name given was not a non-empty string, so nothing was registered and the rows are unfiltered by it.
warnings.fix: Give the predicate a name.

warnings.message: the where predicate "{name}" threw; its rows are treated as not matching:
warnings.meaning: A `where` predicate threw while judging a row. The row is treated as not matching — the fail-closed direction, so a broken predicate hides rows rather than revealing ones it was meant to exclude. The grid keeps filtering; reported once per predicate.
warnings.fix: The error is attached to the console line. The predicate is called with every row's data, including rows whose fields are missing.

warnings.message: find.open(): the find bar is off (config.find is false); grid.find(text) still searches, and find.matches() lists the results.
warnings.meaning: `find.open()` was called with the find UI switched off in the configuration, so no bar appears. The search machinery itself is untouched — the state is still set — so the API-level search continues to work.
warnings.fix: Remove `find: false` to get the bar, or drive the search through `grid.find(text)` and read `find.matches()` yourself.

warnings.message: forecast: holtWinters needs a period (opts.period >= 2)
warnings.meaning: Holt-Winters models a repeating season and cannot do so without knowing how long the season is. With no usable `period` the forecast returns `null` — nothing is drawn and no series is produced.
warnings.fix: Set `period` to the number of observations in one season: 12 for monthly data with a yearly cycle, 7 for daily data with a weekly one.

warnings.message: unrecognised format string "{spec}"; the value will be stringified
warnings.meaning: A format given as a string matched neither the shorthand forms nor anything that reads as a date pattern, so no formatter was compiled. Values render as their plain string form — unrounded, unlocalised, no currency or unit.
warnings.fix: Use one of the shorthands, a date pattern, or a format spec object.

warnings.message: column {col} has format key "{key}", which applies to a {other} column, not the {kind} column it was applied to; it is ignored.
warnings.meaning: The key is a real formatting key — for a different kind of column. A date key on a number column, or a currency key on a text one, has nothing to act on, so it is ignored. This is separated from the unknown-key case because the fix is different: the key is spelt correctly and is on the wrong column.
warnings.fix: Move the key to a column of the kind it applies to, or change the column's type if the type is what is wrong.

warnings.message: format must be a spec object or a string; ignoring
warnings.meaning: The `format` property was neither an object nor a string — a number, an array, a function — so it was ignored entirely and the column formats by its type's defaults. The offending value is attached to the console line.
warnings.fix: Give `format` a spec object or a format string.

warnings.message: column {col} has an unrecognised format key "{key}" for its {kind} format; it is ignored.
warnings.meaning: A key in the format spec is not one the formatter reads, for any kind of column, so it was dropped. Whatever it was meant to control is left at its default — a mis-spelt `minimumFractionDigits` leaves the decimals unconstrained.
warnings.fix: Check the key against the formatting reference.

warnings.message: a scale's "mid" needs an odd number of colours (a middle stop to pin); {n} were given, so "mid" was ignored.
warnings.meaning: `mid` pins the middle colour stop of a colour scale to a particular value, and with an even number of colours there is no middle stop to pin. The setting is ignored and the stops are spread evenly, so a diverging scale will not be centred where you asked.
warnings.fix: Give the scale an odd number of colours — three is the usual diverging scale — or drop `mid`.

warnings.message: a scale's "mid" ({mid}) is outside its min..max range, so it was ignored.
warnings.meaning: The midpoint lies outside the scale's own domain, so there is no position on the ramp to pin it to. The stops are spread evenly instead, and the scale is drawn uncentred.
warnings.fix: Put `mid` between the scale's `min` and `max`, or set the domain explicitly so that it contains the midpoint.

warnings.message: teardown failed
warnings.meaning: One of the grid's registered teardown functions threw while the grid was being destroyed. The throw is caught and the remaining teardown functions still run, so the destruction completes; whatever that one function was meant to release may still be held.
warnings.fix: The error is attached to the console line. A teardown registered by a module or a host hook is the usual source.

warnings.message: edit.addRow was called but this source cannot append rows: it is not a remote source whose adapter declares mutate.append. The row was not added rather than shown on screen and never saved. Use a createPushdownSource over an adapter with mutate: { append: true }.
warnings.meaning: Adding a row optimistically means showing it immediately and reconciling it with what the server says. A source with no append has no server step, so the row would sit on screen for ever and vanish on the next load. It is refused instead, and `null` is returned.
warnings.fix: Use a pushdown source over an adapter that declares `mutate: { append: true }`, or add the row to your own data and reload the grid.

warnings.message: edit.deleteRow was called but this source cannot delete rows: it is not a remote source whose adapter declares mutate.delete. The row was not removed rather than hidden and then reappearing. Use a createPushdownSource over an adapter with mutate: { delete: true }.
warnings.meaning: The mirror of the append case. Without a delete on the adapter the row would disappear from the screen and come back with the next fetch, so the deletion is refused and `null` returned.
warnings.fix: Use a pushdown source over an adapter that declares `mutate: { delete: true }`.

warnings.message: edit.deleteRows (and the Delete-key / "Delete row" gestures) were called but row deletion is off. Set config.rowDelete: true to enable it; deleting data on a keystroke is opt-in. Deletion still flows through beforeDelete so it can be confirmed or vetoed.
warnings.meaning: Row deletion is opt-in: a grid does not remove data because someone pressed a key. With `rowDelete` unset the call — and the Delete-key and context-menu gestures — return an empty array and nothing is deleted.
warnings.fix: Set `rowDelete: true`, and use `beforeDelete` to confirm or veto.
warnings.snippet:
createGrid(el, { rowDelete: true });
grid.on('beforeDelete', (e) => { if (!confirm('Delete?')) e.preventDefault(); });

warnings.message: a '{kind}' rolling column needs an 'orderBy' column to define its order — the screen sort is never used, because a rolling figure would then change on every header click. It reported null until an orderBy is set.
warnings.meaning: A rolling figure — a running total, a moving average, a lag — is defined by an order, and that order is deliberately not the grid's current sort: reading it from the screen would make every cell change when a user clicks a header. With no `orderBy` the figure is undefined, so the column reports `null` for every row.
warnings.fix: Name the column that defines the series order.
warnings.snippet: columns: [{ id: 'runningTotal', rolling: { kind: 'sum', of: 'amount', orderBy: 'date' } }]

warnings.message: a '{kind}' rolling column needs a positive window span (a count of rows, or a time span in ms or 'minutes'); it had none, so the column reported null.
warnings.meaning: The rolling window has no usable size: the span is missing, zero, negative or unparseable. There is no window to reduce over, so the column reports `null` for every row rather than inventing a default width.
warnings.fix: Give the window a positive `span` — a row count, or a time span in milliseconds (or `minutes`).
warnings.snippet: rolling: { kind: 'mean', of: 'price', orderBy: 'at', window: { kind: 'time', minutes: 15 } }

warnings.message: sort ignores an entry with keys { {keys} }; expected { col, dir } (AG Grid's sort model uses "colId"/"direction" — this grid uses "col"/"dir").
warnings.meaning: A sort entry is an object with no usable `col`, so it is dropped from the sort. The other entries still apply. The key carries the entry's own key names, which is what makes the commonest case — an AG Grid sort model handed straight over — recognisable at a glance.
warnings.fix: Use `{ col, dir }`. Translate a migrated sort model: `colId` becomes `col`, `direction` becomes `dir`.

warnings.message: sort ignores unknown column "{col}".
warnings.meaning: A sort entry names a column this grid does not have, so that entry is dropped and the remaining entries are applied. A saved view restored against a different column set is the usual cause.
warnings.fix: Check the column id. A column the user cannot read is also dropped, silently, by the permissions check that follows.

warnings.message: a structural append/delete needs a single-field rowKey so the optimistic row can be rekeyed to the server id; with a composite or function rowKey the temp key cannot be written back onto the row. Set rowKey to one field name to use add-row / delete-row.
warnings.meaning: Adding a row optimistically means giving it a temporary key and then rewriting that key to the id the server assigns. That rewrite needs to know which field holds the key, and a composite or function `rowKey` does not say. The row is still added with its temporary key; it simply cannot be rekeyed when the server answers.
warnings.fix: Set `rowKey` to a single field name for grids that add or delete rows.

warnings.message: a multiplicative decomposition of '{col}' meets a non-positive value, where the ratio value ÷ trend is undefined; those rows report null. Use the additive model for a series that crosses or sits at zero.
warnings.meaning: A multiplicative decomposition divides by the trend, which is meaningless at or below zero. The rows at fault report `null` — the rest of the series is decomposed normally — so the column has gaps where the values touch zero.
warnings.fix: Use the additive model for a series that crosses or sits at zero.

warnings.message: a '{kind}' decomposition column needs a declared integer 'period' of at least 2 (the season length — 7 for a weekly cycle in daily data, say); there is no auto-detection, so it reported null until a period is set.
warnings.meaning: A seasonal decomposition separates a series into trend, season and remainder, and the season length has to be stated: the grid does not guess it. Without a period of at least 2 the column reports `null` for every row.
warnings.fix: Declare the `period` in observations — 7 for a weekly cycle in daily data, 12 for a yearly cycle in monthly data.

warnings.message: config.groupDefaultExpanded threw: {error}; the group starts expanded.
warnings.meaning: The predicate that decides whether a group starts open threw. The group starts expanded — the permissive default — and the grid carries on. Reported once however many groups hit it.
warnings.fix: The error's message is quoted in the line. The predicate is called with a group info object for every group, including empty ones and the ones the grid generates.

warnings.message: grouping by {cols} produced {g} groups for {n} rows: nearly one group per row. Grouping a continuous value such as a percentage or a timestamp rarely reads usefully; consider a computed banding column.
warnings.meaning: The grouping produced almost as many groups as there are rows, which is what happens when a continuous value — a price, a percentage, a timestamp — is used as a grouping key. Nothing is wrong and nothing was refused: the grid grouped exactly as asked, and the result is a tree that is no more readable than the flat rows and considerably slower to draw. Only checked above a hundred rows, so a small grid is never accused.
warnings.fix: Group by a column that bands the value — a computed column that rounds, buckets or names a range — and keep the continuous column for sorting and aggregation.
warnings.snippet: columns: [{ id: 'band', value: { deps: ['amount'], get: (p) => Math.floor(p.data.amount / 1000) * 1000 } }]

warnings.message: applying the {direction} of '{label}' threw.
warnings.meaning: The function that applies a history patch threw while undoing or redoing a step. That step is not applied, so the grid is left between two states: the history position has moved and the state it names was not restored.
warnings.fix: The error is attached to the console line. The label is the one the step was recorded under.

warnings.message: history capture threw; the action was not recorded.
warnings.meaning: The history model captures a snapshot before an action so it can be undone, and the capture function threw. The action still happens; it simply has no undo entry, so undo will step past it to the previous one.
warnings.fix: The error is attached to the console line. The captured value is cloned, so it must be structured-cloneable.

warnings.message: edit {direction} threw; the entry was dropped.
warnings.meaning: History delegates an undo or redo of an edit to the edit model, and that call threw. The entry is dropped from the history rather than retried, so the stack stays consistent and that one step cannot be undone.
warnings.fix: The error is attached to the console line.

warnings.message: message keys not in the catalogue and so ignored: {keys}
warnings.meaning: A message override names keys the catalogue does not contain, so those overrides do nothing. A typo in a translation file is otherwise invisible: the interface simply stays in English and nobody can tell the difference between "not translated" and "translated under the wrong key". Up to five keys are listed, with a count of the rest.
warnings.fix: Check the keys against the default catalogue; the key names are stable and are the ones the grid looks up.

warnings.message: unknown icon set '{name}'; falling back to arrows.
warnings.meaning: A conditional-formatting icon-set rule named a set that does not exist, so the arrows set is used instead. The rule still applies and the thresholds still work; the glyphs are not the ones asked for.
warnings.fix: Use one of the built-in icon set names.

warnings.message: grid.import.apply is synchronous and cannot inflate an .xlsx: await grid.import.xlsx(bytes) for the records (or grid.import.previewXlsx for a preview), then pass those to apply.
warnings.meaning: `apply` is synchronous, and an `.xlsx` is a zip that has to be inflated asynchronously. The bytes were recognised and refused, so nothing was imported and an empty record list was returned.
warnings.fix: Await `grid.import.xlsx(bytes)` (or `previewXlsx`) and pass the records it returns to `apply`.

warnings.message: grid.import.apply was given something it cannot import: pass delimited text, a preview from grid.import.preview, or an array of record objects.
warnings.meaning: The input is none of the three things `apply` takes, so nothing was imported and an empty record list was returned. A `File` or a `Blob` arrives here: both have to be read to text or bytes first.
warnings.fix: Pass delimited text, a preview object, or an array of records.

warnings.message: grid.import.apply changes the grid's own rows, which only a memory-source grid holds. On a remote, paged or stream source the rows come from the backend; import the file there, or load a memory grid from grid.import.csv(text).
warnings.meaning: `import.apply` writes the imported records into the grid's own row set, and only a memory source has one. On any other source the rows come from the backend, so the import is refused and `null` returned rather than producing rows that the next fetch would wipe out.
warnings.fix: Import the file on the server, or build a memory-source grid from the parsed records.

warnings.message: grid.import.xlsx found no worksheet in the .xlsx; nothing to import.
warnings.meaning: The file inflated and parsed, and the workbook names no worksheet the importer can reach. An empty result is returned: no header, no rows, no sheet name. A workbook whose only sheet is a chart sheet looks like this.
warnings.fix: Check the workbook in a spreadsheet application; the importer reads the first ordinary worksheet.

warnings.message: column "{colId}" is an impure computed column (`value.pure: false`) and is being used to {operation}. The result is not stable across passes.
warnings.meaning: A column declared impure — its value may differ between two calls with the same inputs — is being used for an operation that assumes stability, such as sorting, filtering or grouping. The operation still runs; its result simply is not reproducible, so two passes over the same data can order or group the rows differently.
warnings.fix: Make the column pure if it can be (feed the varying input in as data rather than reading it from outside), or keep the impure column for display and operate on a stable one.

warnings.message: column "{colId}" has mixed or ambiguous values and was inferred as "text". Declare `type` on the column to get correct sorting, filtering and export.
warnings.meaning: Informational. The grid sampled the column's values and none of the candidate types matched all of them, so it fell back to `text`. A text column sorts lexically (so 10 comes before 9), filters with text operators, and exports as a string — which is rarely what a column of mixed numbers and blanks was meant to do.
warnings.fix: Declare the column's `type`. The inference is only ever a convenience for data whose shape is not known in advance.

warnings.message: column "{id}" is an impure computed column and is not materialised into the store
warnings.meaning: An impure computation is not a function of the stored data, so there is nothing stable to materialise: the column layer re-evaluates it on every read instead. The column works; it does not get the store's speed, and under `dropSourceRows` it cannot be served at all.
warnings.fix: Nothing, if the impurity is deliberate. Make the column pure — feed the varying input in as data — to have it stored.

warnings.message: column "{id}" holds mixed or unrecognised value types; storing as an object array. Declare a type to avoid this.
warnings.meaning: Informational. Ingest sampled the column and could not settle on a packed representation, so it stores plain object references — correct, and considerably larger and slower than a typed column.
warnings.fix: Declare the column's `type` so ingest can pack it, or clean the data so one type fits.

warnings.message: no licence key supplied. The grid renders in full and carries a trial watermark on any host other than localhost. Get a key at latticegrid.dev.
warnings.meaning: The licence key could not be parsed. The id takes one of two forms — `licence.missing` when no key was supplied at all, and `licence.malformed` when one was supplied and could not be read — and they print different sentences. Either way the grid renders in full: nothing is disabled, and a watermark is drawn on any host other than localhost.
warnings.fix: Supply a valid key in `config.licence`. Development on localhost needs no key.

warnings.message: this host does not provide crypto.subtle Ed25519, so the licence signature could not be verified. A structural check was used instead.
warnings.meaning: Verification needs Ed25519 through `crypto.subtle`, and this runtime does not offer it — an insecure context, or an older browser. The key may well be genuine; this host simply cannot prove it, so only the signature's shape was checked.
warnings.fix: Serve the page over HTTPS (a secure context), which is what `crypto.subtle` requires.

warnings.message: licence key is not valid for {host}; it covers {domains}. The grid will render with a watermark.
warnings.meaning: The key is genuine and is bound to particular domains, and this page is served from another one. It is checked before the signature deliberately: "this key is not for this domain" tells the reader what to do, where a signature failure does not. localhost is always accepted.
warnings.fix: Use a key covering this domain, or serve the application from one of the domains listed in the message. The host compared is the full domain name.

warnings.message: licence expired on {date}. The grid will render with a watermark. Renew at latticegrid.dev.
warnings.meaning: The key is genuine and its expiry date has passed. Nothing is disabled — a build that shipped with a valid key keeps working — and a watermark is drawn.
warnings.fix: Renew the licence and replace the key.

warnings.message: licence key is for '{got}', not '{want}'. The grid will render with a watermark.
warnings.meaning: The key parsed and verifies, and it is for a different product. The grid renders in full with a watermark.
warnings.fix: Use the key issued for this product.

warnings.message: licence signature is not valid. The grid will render with a watermark.
warnings.meaning: The key parsed, its product, dates and domains were checked, and the signature does not verify against the public key. The grid renders in full with a watermark. Verification is entirely offline — nothing is sent anywhere.
warnings.fix: Copy the key again from where it was issued; a truncated or re-wrapped key fails here.

warnings.message: column "{id}" is `layout.lockVisible` and cannot be hidden
warnings.meaning: A hide was refused: the column declares `layout.lockVisible`, which pins it into the visible set. The column stays visible; other columns in the same call are hidden normally.
warnings.fix: Clear `layout.lockVisible` on the column if it should be hideable.

warnings.message: column "{colId}" failed to load lookup options
warnings.meaning: The lookup's options function threw, or the promise it returned rejected. The lookup is left in its error state with no options: values render raw and the editor offers nothing. It is reported once per column, whichever of the two ways it failed.
warnings.fix: The error is attached to the console line. The options function is called once per column and its result cached, so a transient failure leaves the column empty until something re-triggers the load.

warnings.message: column "{colId}" has an invalid `lookup.options`; expected an array or a function
warnings.meaning: `lookup.options` was neither an array of options nor a function returning one (or a promise of one), so there is nothing to look values up in. The lookup resolves to an empty option list: every value renders raw and the select editor has nothing to offer.
warnings.fix: Give `options` an array, or a function that returns one (or a promise of one) for lazy loading.
warnings.snippet: columns: [{ id: 'status', type: 'lookup', lookup: { options: () => fetch('/statuses').then((r) => r.json()) } }]

warnings.message: column "{colId}" holds value {value} which is not in its lookup options. Showing the raw value; set `lookup.unknownLabel` or `lookup.allowCustom` to change that.
warnings.meaning: A row holds a lookup id that the option list does not contain, so there is no label for it and the raw id is shown. It is not reported while the options are still loading — ids that are about to resolve are not a fault — and not at all when `allowCustom` is set, because then a value outside the list is expected.
warnings.fix: Add the value to the options, set `lookup.unknownLabel` to control what an unmatched value shows, or set `lookup.allowCustom` if values outside the list are legitimate.

warnings.message: band "{id}" declares marryChildren, so its columns stay together; the move was ignored
warnings.meaning: The move would have taken a column out of — or through — a band that declares `marryChildren`, which exists precisely to keep its columns adjacent. The move is refused and the order is unchanged. Every route into a move arrives here, so a drag, a keyboard move and the menu command all behave the same way.
warnings.fix: Move the whole band with `columns.moveGroup()`, or drop `marryChildren` from the band.

warnings.message: column "{id}" is not movable; the move was ignored
warnings.meaning: The column declares `layout.movable: false` or `layout.lockPosition`, so the move — from a drag, a keyboard command or the API — was refused and the column order is unchanged.
warnings.fix: Clear the column's `movable`/`lockPosition` layout flags if it should be movable.

warnings.message: unknown filter operator "{op}"; the condition passes every row
warnings.meaning: The filter kernel was given an operator it does not implement. The condition is compiled to a predicate that admits every row, so the filter has no effect — it does not hide anything, and it does not hide everything.
warnings.fix: Use one of the documented operators. A condition built by hand, or restored from an older saved view, is the usual source.

warnings.message: writing a server-authoritative value back threw; the cell may still show the optimistic value.
warnings.meaning: The server confirmed the write with a value of its own — a normalised string, a computed total — and writing that value into the row threw. The cell may still show what the user typed rather than what was stored.
warnings.fix: The error is attached to the console line.

warnings.message: rolling back a rejected write threw; the cell may still show the rejected value.
warnings.meaning: A write was rejected and the rollback itself threw, so the cell may still be showing the value the server refused. The grid's own bookkeeping is unwound either way, so the cell is no longer marked pending — which makes a wrong value look confirmed.
warnings.fix: The error is attached to the console line. Refresh the affected rows if the rollback path can fail in your setup.

warnings.message: an appended row was confirmed without a server key (the adapter's mutate returned no keys and returning is not 'key'/'row'), so the row keeps its client temp key. It is persisted but cannot be addressed by its server id. Declare returning: 'key' or 'row' on the adapter so appended rows can be rekeyed.
warnings.meaning: The append succeeded and the grid never learned the id the server gave the row, so the row keeps the temporary key it was created with. It is saved; it simply cannot be addressed by its real id — a later update or delete keyed on the server id will not find it.
warnings.fix: Declare `returning: 'key'` or `returning: 'row'` on the adapter so the append answers with the new id.

warnings.message: rekeying an appended row from its temp key to the server key threw; selection, expansion, focus or in-flight cell writes on the row may still point at the temp key.
warnings.meaning: The row was saved and the server's id arrived, and moving every reference from the temporary key to the real one threw part of the way through. The engine's own bookkeeping is moved regardless, so what may be left behind is the host-side state listed in the message.
warnings.fix: The error is attached to the console line. Clearing the selection and re-expanding after an append recovers the visible state.

warnings.message: rolling back a rejected structural write threw; the grid may still show the optimistic append or the tombstoned row.
warnings.meaning: A rejected append or delete could not be rolled back. The grid may still be showing a row that was never saved, or hiding a row that was never deleted — the screen and the backend disagree.
warnings.fix: The error is attached to the console line. Reload the rows when a structural rollback fails.

warnings.message: a structural {kind} has been pending for over {n}s ({key}). With edit.confirm "manual" the host must call settle(id, ok); with "auto" the mutate promise never settled.
warnings.meaning: An optimistic append or delete has been waiting beyond the timeout. The row is still shown as pending — an appended row that may never be saved, or a tombstoned row that may come back — until something settles it.
warnings.fix: Settle the operation when your backend answers, or make sure the adapter's mutate promise always settles.

warnings.message: a write has been pending for over {n}s ({key}/{colId}). With edit.confirm "manual" the host must call grid.edit.settle(id, ok); with "auto" the commit promise never settled.
warnings.meaning: An optimistic cell write has been waiting for confirmation beyond the timeout. The cell is still showing the optimistic value and is still marked pending, and it will stay that way until something settles it. Reported once per sweep, naming the oldest offender.
warnings.fix: Under `confirm: 'manual'`, call `grid.edit.settle(id, ok)` when your backend answers. Under `'auto'`, the commit promise must settle — a fetch with no timeout that never rejects produces exactly this.

warnings.message: the permissions callback threw for column "{colId}"; that column and any later failure were treated as "{closed}". Permissions fail closed, so a broken callback removes columns rather than exposing them. This is reported once.
warnings.meaning: The same fault as `permissions.throw:*`, reported by the permissions *model* rather than the default error reporter — and deliberately once per model rather than once per column: a callback that throws throws for every column, and a fifty-column grid must not produce fifty stack traces for one broken function.
