The key is generated per model instance (`perm` followed by a short sequence), which is why it appears in the catalogue as a shape rather than a fixed string. The cost of reporting once is that a callback which only throws for a later column says nothing after the first.
warnings.fix: The error is attached to the console line, and the first report names its column. Fix the callback; every column it throws for is hidden.

warnings.message: {where} is "{value}", which is not one of {levels}; the column was treated as "{closed}" (permissions fail closed)
warnings.meaning: One entry of the permissions policy names a level that does not exist. That column is closed rather than guessed at — the same fail-closed rule as an unreadable policy — so it is hidden. The key names where the bad level came from, so two different entries are two lines.
warnings.fix: Use one of the levels listed in the message. `true` and `false` are accepted as shorthands for the most and least permissive.

warnings.message: config.permissions is a {type}, which is not a level, a map, a list, a callback or a policy object; every column was treated as "hidden" (permissions fail closed)
warnings.meaning: The permissions configuration could not be read as any of the shapes the model accepts. Permissions fail closed, so an unreadable policy hides every column rather than exposing them — the grid will look empty. That is deliberate: the opposite failure would leak data because of a typo.
warnings.fix: Pass a level string, a map of column id to level, a list of levels, a `(params) => level` callback, or a policy object with `resolve`/`entries`/`fallback`.

warnings.message: the permissions callback threw for column "{colId}"; the column was treated as "{closed}". Permissions fail closed, so a broken callback removes columns rather than exposing them.
warnings.meaning: The permissions callback threw while resolving one column. That column is closed, and the reporting is per column, so a callback that throws for one column only names that one.
warnings.fix: The error is attached to the console line. The callback is called for every column, including generated ones such as the auto-group column, which is the usual cause of a first throw.

warnings.message: pivot would generate {n} columns, above the limit of {max}. Pivot on a lower-cardinality column, or raise pivot.maxColumns.
warnings.meaning: The pivot was refused before any columns were built: the number of value columns times the number of distinct pivot values exceeds the limit. No pivot columns are generated and the refusal is returned as the pivot's error, so the grid shows its unpivoted self rather than tens of thousands of columns.
warnings.fix: Pivot on a column with fewer distinct values, narrow the rows with a filter first, or raise `pivot.maxColumns` deliberately.

warnings.message: pivot was given total column ids but no handle(colId) resolver, so no cell values were reduced. Pass values: [{ colId, handle, fn }] or opts.handle.
warnings.meaning: The pivot knows which columns to reduce and has no way to reach their data: the value entries are bare ids and no `handle(colId)` resolver was supplied. No values are reduced, so the pivot draws its structure with empty cells.
warnings.fix: Pass value entries carrying their handles, or supply `opts.handle` so the pivot can resolve them.

warnings.message: presence provider has no subscribe(); peers will never appear.
warnings.meaning: The presence provider does not implement `subscribe`, which is how peers are delivered. Nothing is subscribed, so no peer ever appears and the presence UI stays empty however many people are on the document.
warnings.fix: Implement `subscribe(handler)` on the provider.

warnings.message: setSpotlight was called while no presentation is running, so nothing is dimmed. Start the presentation first, and note that stepping to a view clears the spotlight, so arm it after the deck has started rather than before.
warnings.meaning: The spotlight dims everything but its target, and the painter only dims while a presentation is running. Called on a stopped grid it changes nothing on screen. Stepping to a view also clears the spotlight, so arming it before the deck starts has no effect either.
warnings.fix: Start the presentation, step to the view you want, then set the spotlight.

warnings.message: unknown column preset "{name}"; ignoring
warnings.meaning: A column named a preset that is not registered. It contributes nothing to the resolved column, so the settings the preset would have supplied — a type, a format, an alignment — are all absent and the column falls back to its own definition and the type defaults.
warnings.fix: Register the preset, or name one that exists.
warnings.snippet: createGrid(el, { presets: { money: { type: 'number', format: { style: 'currency' } } } });

warnings.message: print refused: {rows} rows exceeds the ceiling of {max}. Export to Excel or CSV instead
warnings.meaning: Printing lays out every row at once, so a large grid would build a document big enough to hang the tab. The print is refused and `{ printed: false, reason: 'row-ceiling' }` returned; nothing is sent to the printer.
warnings.fix: Filter the grid down, raise `maxRows` deliberately if you accept the cost, or export to Excel or CSV.

warnings.message: unsupported radix {value}; use 2, 8, 16, 'binary', 'octal' or 'hex'. Falling back to hex
warnings.meaning: A radix-formatted column was given a base it does not support. Only the three bases have digit groupings and prefixes defined, so the column renders in hexadecimal instead of the base you asked for.
warnings.fix: Use `2`, `8` or `16`, or the names `'binary'`, `'octal'`, `'hex'`.
warnings.snippet: columns: [{ id: 'flags', type: 'radix', radix: { radix: 2, bitWidth: 16 } }]

warnings.message: unknown radix preset "{name}"; known presets are {list}
warnings.meaning: A radix preset was named and does not exist. The preset contributes nothing, so the column falls back to the radix defaults (or to whatever the surrounding configuration object supplies), which is rarely the rendering the preset was chosen for.
warnings.fix: Use one of the presets listed in the message, or spell the settings out.

warnings.message: signed: false needs a bitWidth to render a two's-complement pattern; defaulting to 32
warnings.meaning: `signed: false` renders a negative number as the bit pattern it would have in a fixed-width register, and without a width there is nothing to complement against. Rather than silently re-signing the value, the formatter picks the commonest width — 32 bits — so a negative number renders as a 32-bit pattern.
warnings.fix: State the `bitWidth` you mean.

warnings.message: unsupported bitWidth {value}; use 8, 16, 32 or 53. Ignoring it
warnings.meaning: The bit width decides how many digits a value is padded to and what a two's-complement rendering complements against, and only those four widths are implemented. The setting is ignored, so values render with no fixed width.

warnings.message: columns.decorate('{id}', …): no column with id '{id}'.
warnings.meaning: `columns.decorate()` named a column that does not exist, so nothing was re-resolved and `undefined` was returned. Nothing on screen changed.
warnings.fix: Check the id against `grid.columns.all()`.

warnings.message: filter operator "matches" received an invalid pattern: {pattern}
warnings.meaning: A `matches` condition's pattern would not compile, so no matcher could be built for it. The condition cannot be evaluated and matches nothing.
warnings.fix: The compilation error is attached to the console line. A `RegExp` object is accepted as well as a string; the `g` and `y` flags are stripped because the matcher is reused across rows.

warnings.message: unknown registry kind '{kind}'; expected one of {list}.
warnings.meaning: `register(kind, name, impl)` was given a kind that does not exist, so nothing was registered. The message lists the kinds that do.
warnings.fix: Use one of the kinds listed in the message.

warnings.message: module '{name}' has no install() and was ignored.
warnings.meaning: The entry has a name and no `install`, so there is nothing to run and the module is not registered. Whatever it provides is absent.
warnings.fix: A module is `{ name, install(ctx) }`. Check that you are passing the module and not, say, its configuration object.

warnings.message: module '{name}' was re-registered with different options; the first registration is kept and this call was ignored. Unregister it first if you mean to replace it.
warnings.meaning: Registration is idempotent by name, because a lazy load may repeat the same registration — so a second call with the *same* options is silent. This one carried different options, which cannot be applied, so the first registration stands and the new options do nothing. Development builds only: a production bundle can neither read nor act on the warning.
warnings.fix: Unregister the module and register it again, or configure it once.

warnings.message: registerModules received something that is not a module; ignored.
warnings.meaning: One of the entries handed to `registerModules` is not an object with a non-empty `name`, so it was skipped. The other entries in the same call are installed normally.
warnings.fix: Pass the module object itself — usually the default export of the module package — rather than its factory or its namespace.

warnings.message: module '{name}' threw during install; it was not registered.
warnings.meaning: `install()` threw, so the module is not registered: anything it would have contributed — renderers, editors, capabilities — is missing, and the grid carries on without it.
warnings.fix: The error is attached to the console line.

warnings.message: module '{name}' threw during uninstall.
warnings.meaning: The module's `uninstall` threw. It is removed from the registry regardless and the capabilities are recomputed, so the grid is consistent; whatever the uninstall was meant to release may still be held.
warnings.fix: The error is attached to the console line.

warnings.message: register('{kind}', ...) needs a name.
warnings.meaning: The kind is valid and the name is missing or is not a string, so there is nothing to register under and nothing was registered.
warnings.fix: Pass a non-empty string name.

warnings.message: a registry change handler threw.
warnings.meaning: One of the registry's change listeners threw. Delivery continues to the others and the registry change itself is unaffected.
warnings.fix: The error is attached to the console line.

warnings.message: '{name}' was already registered as a {kind} and has been replaced.
warnings.meaning: A different implementation was registered under a name that was already taken, and it replaced the previous one — the registration succeeds. It is reported because the replacement is global to the grid: everything that resolves that name now gets the new implementation, including code you did not write. Re-registering the *same* implementation is silent.
warnings.fix: Register under a name of your own if the replacement was not intended.

warnings.message: column "{id}" is not resizable; the resize was ignored
warnings.meaning: The column declares `layout.resizable: false`, so the new width — from a drag or from the API — was refused and the column keeps its width.
warnings.fix: Clear `layout.resizable: false` on the column if it should be resizable.

warnings.message: rowHeight function threw; the default height was used.
warnings.meaning: The per-row height function threw, so that row is laid out at the default height. The grid keeps rendering; a row that should have been taller is clipped.
warnings.fix: The error is attached to the console line. The function is called for every row, including group rows, and must return a positive number — anything else also falls back to the default, silently.

warnings.message: rowKey {named} is missing on {n} of {m} rows; the first such row has: {fields}. Rows without a key value collapse onto one key, so selection, edits and rows.apply updates land on whichever row now shares it. Set rowKey to a field present on every row, or fix the source data.
warnings.meaning: The key field is absent (or empty) on some rows, and every one of those rows produces the same key. They are therefore the *same row* as far as the grid is concerned: selecting one selects them all, an edit lands on whichever the lookup finds first, and an incoming update for that key overwrites an arbitrary one. The message names the fields the first offending row does have, which is usually enough to see what went wrong.
warnings.fix: Use a field that is present on every row, or fix the data so the key is always there.

warnings.message: no rowKey configured, so rows are identified by object identity. This disables: {features}. Set rowKey to a field name, an array of field names, or a function.
warnings.meaning: Without a `rowKey` the grid identifies a row by the object it was handed, which works only as long as that exact object stays in place. Everything that has to recognise the same row across a reload, a sort or an incoming delta is switched off; the message lists them by name.
warnings.fix: Set `rowKey` to the field that identifies a row, an array of fields for a composite key, or a function returning one.

warnings.message: rowKey function threw; falling back to index identity for the affected rows.
warnings.meaning: The `rowKey` function threw for a row, so that row is keyed by its index instead. An index key is not stable across a sort, a filter or a reload, so selection, editing and live updates on that row will behave as though it had no key at all.
warnings.fix: The error is attached to the console line. The function is called for every row, including ones whose fields are missing.

warnings.message: rows.forEachAll walked only the rows this source has loaded: a remote or paged source holds the current page, not the whole set. Total on the server, or use a memory source.
warnings.meaning: `forEachAll` means "every row, filters ignored", and a source that fetches on demand does not hold every row. The walk covered what is loaded. This is said out loud rather than quietly handing back a subset, because a caller who asked for everything and silently received part of it computes a number that looks right.
warnings.fix: Compute the figure where the whole set is — on the server, or through the adapter — or hold the data in a memory source.

warnings.message: rows.forEachExcept fell back to the filtered rows: this source cannot exclude one column's filter, so the result is narrowed by the column you asked to leave out.
warnings.meaning: `forEachExcept` exists so that a facet or cross-filter panel can show the counts that would apply if its own filter were lifted. A source that fetches on demand cannot answer that question, so the walk falls back to the ordinary filtered rows — which *are* narrowed by the very column you asked to exclude. A cross-filtering panel on that fallback collapses to the single value the user just clicked, which is exactly the failure the exclusion prevents.
warnings.fix: Cross-filtering needs a memory source. On a remote or paged source, exclude the column's filter in your own query instead.

warnings.message: rows.leavesOf() needs a source that groups in memory; this grid groups elsewhere, so it returned no rows.
warnings.meaning: `leavesOf(key)` hands back the leaf rows under a group row, which the grid can only do when it did the grouping itself. This grid groups in the adapter or on the server, so the leaves are not held locally and an empty array is returned.
warnings.fix: Use a memory source, or fetch the group's rows yourself with the group's own key as the query.

warnings.message: selection is being tracked by index because no rowKey is configured; it will not survive a sort, filter or reload.
warnings.meaning: With no `rowKey` the selection is a set of positions rather than a set of rows. Sorting, filtering or reloading moves the rows and leaves the positions where they were, so the user finds different rows selected than the ones they chose.
warnings.fix: Configure `rowKey`.

warnings.message: a 'history' shadow's 'window' only accepts {kind: 'time', span}; '{kind}' is not honoured (a plain count is already what 'depth' means, and a session has no span to divide into buckets), so it reported the original, unwindowed history.
warnings.meaning: A history shadow keeps the recent values of a cell, and a window over it can only be a time window: a count is what `depth` already means, and a session has no span to bucket. The window is ignored and the shadow reports its full, unwindowed history.
warnings.fix: Use `{ kind: 'time', span }` (or `minutes`), or set `depth` for a plain count of readings.

warnings.message: a 'history' shadow's time window needs a positive 'span' (ms) or 'minutes'; it had none, so it reported the original, unwindowed history.
warnings.meaning: The window is a time window and has no usable length, so there is nothing to bucket the readings into. The shadow reports its full history instead.
warnings.fix: Give the window a positive `span` in milliseconds, or `minutes`.

warnings.message: config.context is not JSON-serialisable; cache keys ignore it.
warnings.meaning: `context` is part of what makes a fetch unique, so it goes into the cache key. This one cannot be serialised — a function, a circular structure, a `Map` — so the key is computed without it. Two requests differing only in their context now look like the same request and one may be served from the other's cached result.
warnings.fix: Keep `context` to plain JSON-serialisable data.

warnings.message: a derived grid is deriving from itself, directly or through a chain. The cycle was refused; check the `from` of each grid in the chain.
warnings.meaning: A derived grid may itself be the source of another — a profile *of* the top five is a real request — so a cycle is reachable, and a cycle here would recurse until the stack ran out rather than merely producing a wrong answer. The derivation is refused and the grid keeps whatever rows it had.
warnings.fix: Check the `from` of every grid in the chain; one of them points back.

warnings.message: unknown follow "{mode}"; using "filtered". Known: {list}.
warnings.meaning: `follow` decides which of the parent's rows the derived grid sees — everything, what the filters leave, what is selected. The value is not one of them, so `filtered` is used: the derived grid follows the parent's filters, which is the common case but may not be the one you meant.
warnings.fix: Use one of the modes listed in the message.

warnings.message: source.mode "derived" needs `from`: the grid to derive from.
warnings.meaning: A derived source computes its rows from another grid, and none was named — or, for a union, the array of parents resolved to nothing usable. The source is inert: it produces no rows at all.
warnings.fix: Set `from` to the grid instance to derive from, or to an array of `{ grid, label }` entries for a union.
warnings.snippet: createGrid(el, { source: { mode: 'derived', from: parentGrid, follow: 'filtered' } });

warnings.message: source.mode "derived": `profile` and `statistics` are both terminal producers and cannot be used together — each replaces the pipeline with its own output builder. Declare one, or chain a second derived grid whose `from` is the first.
warnings.meaning: A terminal producer replaces the derivation pipeline with its own output, so two of them have no combined meaning: a profile of the correlations is a different derivation, not a merged one. The configuration is refused and no rows are produced.
warnings.fix: Declare one producer. To do both, chain a second derived grid whose `from` is the first.

warnings.message: source.mode "derived": `{producer}` is a terminal producer and replaces the pipeline, so {keys} {is|are} ignored. Sort, filter or limit the derived grid itself, or chain a second derived grid whose `from` is this one.
warnings.meaning: A terminal producer builds its own output, so the pipeline keys listed in the message never run. They are ignored rather than silently reordering the producer's output, which would give a different answer from the one they describe.
warnings.fix: Sort, filter or limit the derived grid itself — its own query applies to the producer's output — or chain a second derived grid.

warnings.message: a derived grid is read-only: its rows are computed from another grid. Write to the source grid instead, and the derived one follows.
warnings.meaning: A change was applied to a derived source. Its rows are computed, so there is nothing to write into and no way to invert the computation back onto the parent's rows: every operation in the change is rejected, and the rejections are reported back to the caller.
warnings.fix: Write to the source grid; the derived grid recomputes from it.

warnings.message: source.mode "derived": `statistics: { fn: 'correlation' }` needs `columns`: at least two column ids to correlate pairwise.
warnings.meaning: A correlation is between pairs of columns, and fewer than two were named. Nothing is produced.
warnings.fix: Name at least two column ids in `columns`.

warnings.message: source.mode "derived": unknown `statistics.fn` "{fn}". Known: {list}. Every *single-column* statistic is reached through `select` instead, e.g. `select: { p95: { of: 'amount', fn: 'p95' } }`.
warnings.meaning: `statistics` names the *relational* statistics — the ones whose answer is a table of relationships between columns or datasets. The name given is not one of them, so nothing is produced. A single-column statistic is not here at all; it is a `select` entry.
warnings.fix: Use one of the relational statistics listed in the message, or reach a single-column statistic through `select`.

warnings.message: source.mode "derived": unknown `statistics.orient` "{orient}" for `fn: 'correlation'`; using "pairs". Known: pairs, matrix.
warnings.meaning: `orient` chooses the shape of the correlation output — one row per pair, or a square matrix. The value is neither, so `pairs` is used and the grid's columns will be the pairwise shape rather than the matrix one.
warnings.fix: Use `'pairs'` or `'matrix'`.

warnings.message: source.mode "derived": `statistics: { fn: 'series' }` needs both `of` (the column to summarise) and `by` (the column that orders it). `by` is never guessed — kernels see rows in arrival order, which is not the grid's sort.
warnings.meaning: A series statistic summarises one column along the order of another, and one of the two is missing. The order is never guessed: the kernels see rows in arrival order, which is not what the grid is showing, so a guessed order would silently produce a different series from the one on screen. Nothing is produced.
warnings.fix: Name both `of` and `by`.

warnings.message: source.mode "derived": `statistics` needs an object naming the statistic, e.g. `{ fn: 'correlation', columns: ['a', 'b'] }`. Known fn: {list}.
warnings.meaning: `statistics` was not an object, so no statistic could be built and the derived grid produces no rows.
warnings.fix: Pass an object naming the statistic and its arguments.
warnings.snippet: source: { mode: 'derived', from: grid, statistics: { fn: 'correlation', columns: ['price', 'volume'] } }

warnings.message: source.mode "derived": `statistics: { fn: 'datasetVsDataset' }` needs `with`: the second grid to compare this one against.
warnings.meaning: A dataset-versus-dataset comparison needs two datasets and only one was given. Nothing is produced.
warnings.fix: Set `with` to the second grid.

warnings.message: source.mode "derived": `crossFilter` is not supported when `from` is a union of several grids (BACKLOG-0001045) — it has no single target once there is more than one parent. Push a filter onto the individual source grid you mean instead.
warnings.meaning: Cross-filtering pushes a filter back onto the parent, and a union has several. The option does nothing. It is reported at construction rather than when `crossFilter` is first used, so that a host that configures it and never calls it still learns that the line has no effect.
warnings.fix: Push the filter onto the individual source grid you mean.

warnings.message: source.mode "derived": union source "{label}" was refused — it derives from the grid being derived, directly or through a chain ({path}). Remove it from `from`.
warnings.meaning: One parent of the union derives, directly or through a chain, from the grid doing the deriving. That entry is refused and the rest of the union works; the message prints the chain so the loop can be seen.
warnings.fix: Remove that entry from `from`, or break the chain it names.

warnings.message: source.mode "derived": union source "{label}" failed to read ({error}) and was skipped this pass.
warnings.meaning: Reading one parent threw — usually in its `map` function, or in the parent grid itself — so that parent contributes no rows to this pass. The union still delivers the others, so the grid shows a partial set rather than nothing.
warnings.fix: The error's message is quoted in the line. A `map` that assumes a field the parent does not always carry is the usual cause.

warnings.message: source.mode "derived": `follow` is ignored when `from` is a union of several grids (BACKLOG-0001045) — each entry carries its own `follow` instead.
warnings.meaning: In a union each parent decides for itself how much of its grid to contribute, so a single top-level `follow` has nothing to apply to. It is ignored and each entry's own `follow` is used.
warnings.fix: Put `follow` on each entry of the `from` array.
warnings.snippet: from: [{ grid: a, label: 'A', follow: 'filtered' }, { grid: b, label: 'B', follow: 'all' }]

warnings.message: source.mode "derived": two union sources share the label "{label}"; give each a distinct `label` or __source/__key will not distinguish them.
warnings.meaning: Each union entry stamps its rows with its label, and that label is how a row's origin is told — and how its key is made unique across parents. Two entries sharing one label make their rows indistinguishable: `__source` no longer says which grid a row came from, and two rows with the same id from different parents collide.
warnings.fix: Give each entry of `from` a distinct `label`.

warnings.message: source.mode "derived": union source "{label}" has no grid and was skipped.
warnings.meaning: One entry of the union names no grid, so it contributes no rows. The entry is kept in the list — so its label stays reserved — and the other parents union normally.
warnings.fix: Give the entry a `grid`, or remove it from `from`.

warnings.message: source.mode "derived": `profile` is not supported when `from` is a union of several grids (BACKLOG-0001045); profile a single grid instead.
warnings.meaning: As with `statistics`: a profile describes one grid's own columns. Over a union it is refused rather than guessed at, and no rows are produced by it.
warnings.fix: Profile a single grid.

warnings.message: source.mode "derived": `statistics` is not supported when `from` is a union of several grids (BACKLOG-0001046) — a relational statistic reduces one grid's own columns, and a union has no single set of them. Derive the statistics of a single grid instead.
warnings.meaning: A relational statistic is computed over one grid's columns, and a union has as many column sets as it has parents. The option does nothing and the union produces its ordinary unioned rows.
warnings.fix: Derive the statistics of a single grid, and union the results if you need several.

warnings.message: a DFQL update tried to write protected field(s) {fields}; they are server-assigned and immutable, so they were dropped from the PATCH.
warnings.meaning: The listed fields are assigned by the server and cannot be written. They were removed from the PATCH and the rest of the update was sent, so the write succeeded — without those fields.
warnings.fix: Do not include the server-assigned fields in an update; a grid column over one of them should be read-only.

warnings.message: column "{colId}" cannot be served under ingest.dropSourceRows: it is an impure computed column (a shadow or a positional/rank column) that is never stored, so it can only be read from the caller's row objects
warnings.meaning: `ingest.dropSourceRows` frees the original row objects once their values are columnised, and an impure computed column — a shadow, a rank, anything positional — is never stored, so it can only be read from the objects that are now gone. Rather than hand back a handle full of `undefined` and quietly sort, filter or total the grid to a wrong answer, no handle is returned at all and the caller drops the column through its usual unknown-column path.
warnings.fix: Keep the source rows (`ingest.dropSourceRows: false`) if the column is needed, or drop the column.

warnings.message: a prepared statement against "{from}" could not be closed. The query itself succeeded, so this is a resource leak in the engine connection rather than a wrong answer — but a connection that cannot close statements will eventually refuse to prepare new ones.
warnings.meaning: The query ran and returned the right rows; only the cleanup failed. Statements accumulate on the connection, and once the engine's statement limit is reached no further query can be prepared — at which point the grid stops loading entirely.
warnings.fix: This is a driver or connection problem rather than a query one. Re-creating the connection clears the accumulated statements.

warnings.message: the count statement against "{from}" returned no readable count, so the grid has no total for this query and will scroll open-ended rather than show the page size as the whole. This is an engine or driver result-shape problem, not a query problem.
warnings.meaning: The count query ran and its result could not be read as a number. The total is left absent rather than defaulting to the page length, so the grid scrolls open-ended.
warnings.fix: A driver returning counts in an unexpected shape is the cause; check the driver version.

warnings.message: DESCRIBE of "{from}" failed ({error}), so filter values are typed from the grid column types alone. A timestamp or date filter on a column whose grid type is not declared may be refused by the engine.
warnings.meaning: The adapter uses `DESCRIBE` to learn the engine's own column types so that it can bind filter values with the right SQL type. Without it, types come from the grid's column declarations alone — which is enough for a declared column and not enough for an undeclared one, where a date or timestamp comparison may be rejected by the engine.
warnings.fix: Declare the `type` on the grid columns you filter, or fix whatever made `DESCRIBE` fail (the error is quoted in the message).

warnings.message: this DuckDB connection has no prepare(), so filter values cannot be bound. Filters are not sent rather than being interpolated into SQL.
warnings.meaning: Filter values are bound as parameters, never interpolated into SQL text — that is what keeps a value containing a quote from becoming an injection. This connection cannot prepare statements, so the filtered query was not sent at all and no rows are returned.
warnings.fix: Use a connection that implements `prepare()`. Every supported DuckDB-WASM build does.

warnings.message: this DuckDB connection has no prepare(), so filter values cannot be bound. Aggregates are not pushed rather than being interpolated into SQL.
warnings.meaning: The same refusal for whole-set aggregates: none are pushed down, so totals and statistics that would have been computed by the engine are absent.
warnings.fix: Use a connection that implements `prepare()`.

warnings.message: this DuckDB connection has no prepare(), so filter values cannot be bound. A grouped level is not fetched rather than having its values interpolated into SQL.
warnings.meaning: The same refusal on the grouping path: a level of the group tree could not be fetched, so that branch stays empty.
warnings.fix: Use a connection that implements `prepare()`.

warnings.message: this DuckDB connection has no prepare(), so filter values cannot be bound. Grouped aggregates are not pushed rather than being interpolated into SQL.
warnings.meaning: Grouped aggregates could not be pushed down, so no group-level aggregate values come back from the engine and the group rows show none.
warnings.fix: Use a connection that implements `prepare()`.

warnings.message: {url} was asked for totalCount and answered without one, so the grid has no total for this query and will scroll open-ended rather than present the page size as the whole. The schema may not expose totalCount on this connection; pass `count: false` to stop asking, or a `parseResponse` that reads whatever the schema does call it.
warnings.meaning: The adapter asked for a total and the response carries none. Treating the page length as the whole set would be a confident, wrong number, so the total is left absent and the grid scrolls open-ended instead.
warnings.fix: Pass `count: false` to stop asking, or a `parseResponse` that reads whatever your schema calls the total.

warnings.message: the graphql adapter was built without `fields` or `selection`, so the default query selects only `id`. Name the fields your grid shows, or pass a custom `buildQuery`.
warnings.meaning: A GraphQL query has to name the fields it wants, and the adapter was told none. It asks for `id` alone, so every other column in the grid reads `undefined` — the request succeeds and the grid looks empty.
warnings.fix: Pass `fields` (an array of names) or `selection` (a raw selection set), or build the query yourself with `buildQuery`.

warnings.message: grouping ignores unknown column "{col}".
warnings.meaning: A `groupBy` entry names a column the source cannot read, so that level is dropped from the grouping. The remaining levels still group, so the tree is shallower than asked for rather than absent.
warnings.fix: Check the column id in `groupBy`.

warnings.message: unknown source.mode "{mode}"; falling back to "memory". Known modes: {list}.
warnings.meaning: The source mode is not one the grid implements, so a memory source was built instead. Everything the intended mode would have done — fetching, paging, streaming, deriving — does not happen, and the grid shows only the rows it was handed directly.
warnings.fix: Use one of the modes listed in the message.

warnings.message: rows.move() is not supported under ingest.dropSourceRows: the source objects have been released and the store cannot reorder its columns in place. Enable retainSource (leave dropSourceRows off) to reorder rows.
warnings.meaning: Reordering rows means reordering the array they live in, and under `dropSourceRows` there is no array: the store holds the data columnwise. Reordering columns row by row is a different operation the store does not offer, so the move is refused loudly rather than doing nothing quietly — or, worse, corrupting the physical indexing the store keys on.
warnings.fix: Leave `ingest.dropSourceRows` off for a grid whose rows can be reordered.

warnings.message: {base} was asked for $count=true and answered without an @odata.count, so the grid has no total for this query and will scroll open-ended rather than present the page size as the whole. The endpoint does not support $count, or filters it out.
warnings.meaning: `$count=true` was sent and the service answered without a count — the endpoint ignoring an OData directive. As with the GraphQL case, the total is left absent rather than invented from the page length.
warnings.fix: Turn the count off for this endpoint if it cannot answer it, or fix the service so `$count` is honoured.

warnings.message: source.mode "paged" requires a fetch function; the grid will stay empty.
warnings.meaning: A paged source asks for a window of rows at a time and was given no way to ask. No fetch is ever made and the grid shows nothing at all.
warnings.fix: Supply `source.fetch`.
warnings.snippet: source: { mode: 'paged', fetch: ({ start, end }) => api.page(start, end) }

warnings.message: off-thread sort failed; recomputed on the main thread.
warnings.meaning: The sort was offloaded to the worker and failed there, so it was re-run on the main thread and the model settled normally. The rows are correct; this pass cost the round trip and the main-thread time.
warnings.fix: The error is attached to the console line. A repeated failure usually means the worker cannot load the compute kernels — see `worker/no-compute`.

warnings.message: pivot requested but ctx.compute.pivot is not available; showing unpivoted rows.
warnings.meaning: Pivoting is done by a compute kernel and this build has none loaded, so the pivot is skipped and the grid shows its ordinary rows and columns.
warnings.fix: This is a packaging shape: the compute kernels must be reachable. Importing the grid from the published bundle rather than a hand-assembled subset is the reliable route.

warnings.message: createPushdownSource needs an `adapter` with an `execute(query)` function.
warnings.meaning: The pushdown source has nothing to push to. A remote source is still returned so the grid builds, and its fetch answers with no rows and a total of zero — the grid is permanently empty.
warnings.fix: Pass an adapter with `execute(query)` and a `capabilities` declaration.

warnings.message: the {adapter} adapter cannot compute {grouped }aggregates, so every requested statistic is computed client-side. Correct, and slower than it needs to be.
warnings.meaning: The adapter implements neither `executeAggregates` nor — for a grouped query — `executeGroupedAggregates`, so no statistic is pushed at all: the whole set falls to the client rather than half of it being pushed. The figures are right and every one of them costs a full fetch.
warnings.fix: Implement the aggregate method on the adapter. The id carries a `.grouped` suffix when it was the grouped variant that was missing.

warnings.message: the {adapter} adapter was not asked to group this query because {reason}. The engine returns rows and the grouping is the grid's to do, which needs every matching row in the browser — correct where the grid holds them, and wrong-looking where it holds a window. `lastPlan().unpushed` names it.
warnings.meaning: Grouping was not pushed for the reason named. The grid groups what it holds: right when it holds every matching row, and visibly wrong — group counts and subtotals describing a page — when it holds only a window.
warnings.fix: The reason is printed in the message and is also in `lastPlan().unpushed`. Widen the adapter, or arrange for the grid to hold the whole set.

warnings.message: the {adapter} adapter declares the `group` capability but has no `executeGroupLevel(query, aggregates, request)`, so grouping is not pushed and the grid is left to group whatever rows it holds. Implement the method or drop the capability.
warnings.meaning: A capability declared without the method behind it is the one thing the planner cannot see — it is handed capabilities, not the adapter. The query is re-planned without grouping, so `lastPlan()` reports the query that actually ran and names `group` among the unpushed work, and the grid groups whatever rows it has.
warnings.fix: Implement `executeGroupLevel`, or stop declaring the `group` capability.

warnings.message: the {adapter} adapter cannot compute the group subtotal for {columns}, so those group rows carry no value for that column. A figure computed over anything other than the group would be wrong, so none is shown; `lastPlan().aggregates.client` names them.
warnings.meaning: A group subtotal has to be computed over the group's own rows, which the grid does not hold under pushdown grouping. Rather than show a figure computed over something else, the group rows are left empty for those columns. The message names each column and why it could not be pushed.
warnings.fix: Teach the adapter the aggregate, or use a reduction it supports. `lastPlan().aggregates.client` lists them programmatically.

warnings.message: the {adapter} adapter could not count the unfiltered set ({error}), so "N of M" falls back to the display count for its denominator.
warnings.meaning: The unfiltered count is the denominator in "N of M rows". The adapter's count failed, so the denominator falls back to the displayed count — which makes "N of M" read as though nothing were filtered out.
warnings.fix: The error's message is quoted in the line. Implement `unfilteredCount()` on the adapter, or fix whatever made it fail.

warnings.message: the {adapter} adapter returned {n} of {total} matching rows when asked for the whole result. The adapter must follow the engine's own paging before returning.
warnings.meaning: The adapter was asked for the whole result and answered with part of it, and there is no residual work to do — so the rows that came back are correct as far as they go and the set is short. That is a broken adapter rather than a wrong answer, and it is said once.
warnings.fix: Make the adapter follow the engine's own paging and return every row it was asked for.

warnings.message: the {adapter} adapter returned {n} of {total} matching rows when asked for the whole result, and residual work will run over that fraction. allowPartialResults is set, so the result is used as-is — it may be wrong. The adapter must follow the engine's own paging to be correct.
warnings.meaning: The same shortfall, with filtering or sorting still to do in the browser — so the residual work runs over a fraction of the result and can return the wrong rows. Without `allowPartialResults` this case throws; with it, the permissive path is taken and the hazard is named once.
warnings.fix: Fix the adapter's paging, hold the data in memory, or keep `allowPartialResults` knowingly.

warnings.message: edit is enabled but the {adapter} adapter declares mutate: {false|without update} (read-only by declaration), so no commit is synthesised and the grid stays read-only. Declare `mutate: { update: true }` on the adapter to allow cell edits.
warnings.meaning: Editing was configured over an adapter that declares itself read-only. No commit hook is synthesised, so the grid stays read-only rather than accepting edits that could never be persisted.
warnings.fix: Declare `mutate: { update: true }` on the adapter, or supply your own `edit.commit`.

warnings.message: the {adapter} adapter cannot push {work}, so every matching row is fetched and the rest is applied in the browser. Correct, and slower than it needs to be: widening the adapter is the fix.
warnings.meaning: Part of the query could not be expressed to the engine, so the grid asks for every matching row and finishes the work locally. The answer is right; the cost is the full download on every query. The key carries the adapter and exactly which work was left over, so two different shortfalls are two lines.
warnings.fix: Widen the adapter to handle the named work, or narrow the query to what it can push. `lastPlan().unpushed` names it programmatically.

warnings.message: unknown relative date token "{token}"; sending the condition unresolved.
warnings.meaning: A relative date token could not be turned into a concrete date range, so the condition is sent to the source exactly as written. Whether that means anything depends on the adapter: most will not understand the token, and the condition will either be ignored or rejected.
warnings.fix: Use one of the relative tokens listed in the message.

warnings.message: source.mode "remote" requires a fetch function; the grid will stay empty.
warnings.meaning: A remote source delegates sorting, filtering and grouping to the server, and it has no way to reach one. No request is ever made and the grid stays empty.
warnings.fix: Supply `source.fetch`.

warnings.message: config.hostFilter is not sent to a server-delegated source (paged/remote) and is not applied: filtering only the fetched window would give wrong counts and totals. Express the filter as a FilterSet condition, or send it through config.context.
warnings.meaning: A `hostFilter` is application logic the grid cannot serialise, so it cannot be sent to a server. Applying it locally would filter only the rows already fetched, which makes the count, the totals and the scroll length all describe a different set from the one on screen — so it is not applied at all.
warnings.fix: Express the narrowing as a declarative filter condition the source can send, or pass whatever the server needs through `config.context`.

warnings.message: no config.rowKey; falling back to index identity. Row changes, streaming dedupe, selection persistence and remote reload are disabled.
warnings.meaning: The source needs a stable identity per row to deduplicate a stream, to match an incoming change, and to keep a selection across a reload. Without `rowKey` a row is identified by its position, which changes whenever the rows do, so each of those features is switched off.
warnings.fix: Set `rowKey` to the field that identifies a row.

warnings.message: sort ignores unknown column "{col}".
warnings.meaning: A sort entry names a column the source has no data handle for, so that entry is dropped. With a single-entry sort the rows come back unsorted; with several, the remaining entries still apply.
warnings.fix: Check the column id in the sort.

warnings.message: sort ignores "{col}": a running total is a function of the sort order, so it cannot also decide it. Sort by the column it runs over instead.
warnings.meaning: A running total is computed along the current order, so sorting by it would define the order in terms of itself — a question with no fixed point. The entry is dropped, the way an unknown column is, and the rest of the sort applies.
warnings.fix: Sort by the column the running total runs over, or by its `orderBy` column.

warnings.message: worker columnization failed; columnizing on the main thread
warnings.meaning: The worker was asked to columnise a chunk and failed, so the chunk was columnised on the main thread and the worker path is ruled out for the rest of this stream. No rows are lost. A superseded request during a reload is normal and is not reported.
warnings.fix: The error is attached to the console line.

warnings.message: stream ingest.useWorker is on but a column reads through a closure (a computed or date column); columnizing on the main thread instead.
warnings.meaning: Informational. Columnising off-thread needs a schema that can cross the worker boundary, and a column that reads through a closure — a computed column, or a date column with a `toStorage` — cannot. The schema will not change mid-stream, so the worker path is ruled out once rather than probed for every chunk, and ingest runs on the main thread.
warnings.fix: Nothing is wrong. To get the off-thread path, express the column's reading declaratively rather than as a function.

warnings.message: source.mode "stream" requires an open function; the grid will stay empty.
warnings.meaning: A stream source is driven by an `open` function that starts the feed and pushes rows in. Without one nothing ever starts and no row ever arrives.
warnings.fix: Supply `source.open`.
warnings.snippet: source: { mode: 'stream', open: ({ push }) => { const ws = new WebSocket(url); ws.onmessage = (e) => push([JSON.parse(e.data)]); return () => ws.close(); } }

warnings.message: removing rows from a live stream is not supported; reload instead.
warnings.meaning: A change carrying removals was applied to a stream source. The additions in the same change are applied; the removals are not, so those rows stay on screen. A stream is an append-and-evict structure, and removing an arbitrary row from the middle of it is not an operation it offers.
warnings.fix: Reload the stream to drop rows, or let the rolling window evict them.

warnings.message: ctx.compute.testValue is unavailable; streamed rows are not filtered client-side.
warnings.meaning: A stream applies the grid's filters to each arriving row using the compute kernel's value test, and the kernel is not loaded. Every arriving row is admitted, so rows the filters should have excluded appear as they arrive.
warnings.fix: As with the pivot kernel, this is a packaging shape: the compute kernels must be reachable from the bundle you ship.

warnings.message: skipping a malformed NDJSON line (line {n}) from {url} — {error}
warnings.meaning: A line of the NDJSON file would not parse and the source is in lenient mode, so the line is skipped and the rest of the file continues to load. Strict mode throws instead. Reported once per URL, so a file with a thousand bad lines produces one line and loses a thousand rows.
warnings.fix: Fix the file, or keep lenient mode knowingly. The line number and the parse error are quoted so the offending record can be found.

warnings.message: createUrlSource needs a URL string; the grid will stay empty.
warnings.meaning: The URL source was constructed with no URL, so there is nothing to fetch and no rows are ever produced.
warnings.fix: Pass the URL as the first argument.

warnings.message: filters.where("{name}") is registered but the {mode} source holds only its fetched window and cannot run the predicate over it: the predicate is not applied there, and rows it would exclude stay on screen. Give it a { condition } twin so the engine can narrow the fetch itself — that is the supported route for a paged or remote source.
warnings.meaning: Stronger than the page-relative case: this source cannot run the predicate at all, so it is not applied and the rows it would have excluded are visible. The grid is showing more than the predicate says it should.
warnings.fix: Give the predicate a `{ condition }` twin so the narrowing is done by the engine.

warnings.message: filters.where ({names}) is not applied to the {adapter} pushdown source: {the size of the matching set is unknown|its matching set is N rows, at or past the whereRowLimit}. Running the predicate needs every matching row fetched and held here, which is the whole download a pushdown source exists to avoid, so it is refused and the rows the predicate would exclude stay on screen.
warnings.meaning: Running a function predicate over a pushdown source means fetching every matching row into the browser — the download the source exists to avoid. Past `whereRowLimit` (or when the size is unknown) that is refused, so the predicate does not run and the rows it would have hidden stay on screen. The key carries the adapter's name, so two sources on one page are two separate silences.
warnings.fix: Give the predicate a `{ condition }` twin so the engine narrows the fetch — that works at any size — or raise `whereRowLimit` on the source config if you do want the download.

warnings.message: filters.where ({names}) runs over the rows the {mode} source fetched, not the whole dataset: match counts and totals are page-relative. Give the predicate a { condition } twin so the engine can narrow the fetch itself.
warnings.meaning: The predicate does run — over the window this source has fetched. Every row on screen is judged, and the counts and totals describe that window rather than the dataset, so a figure read off the grid is page-relative.
warnings.fix: Register the predicate with a `{ condition }` twin: the grid pushes the condition to the source so the narrowing happens where the whole set is, and runs your function locally as the authority.
warnings.snippet: grid.filters.where('mine', fn, { condition: { colId: 'owner', op: 'eq', value: me } });

warnings.message: `{stat}` on `{col}` (source #{n}) computed over {covered} of {total} matching rows (windowed source); hold the data in a memory source for whole-dataset statistics.
warnings.meaning: The statistic was computed over the rows this windowed source is holding, not over every row that matches. The number is real and it is a sample: it describes the window, not the dataset. The message carries the coverage so you can judge how far off it might be. Development builds only; the key is the statistic and the column, so a long session cannot grow the de-duplication set.
warnings.fix: Hold the data in a memory source for an exact figure, or compute the statistic where the whole set lives — on the server, or in the adapter through pushdown.

warnings.message: duplicate column id "{id}" in the store schema; ignoring the second
warnings.meaning: Two schema entries share an id. The first is kept and the second ignored, so whatever the second declared — a different kind, a different reader — is not in effect.
warnings.fix: Give each column a distinct id in the ingest schema.

warnings.message: column "{id}" declares unknown storage kind "{kind}"; falling back to object
warnings.meaning: The column store packs values by kind — typed arrays for numbers, a dictionary for repeated strings, a bitset for booleans — and this kind is not one it implements. The column is stored as a plain object array, which is correct and uses considerably more memory than the typed form would.
warnings.fix: Use one of the storage kinds the store implements, or leave the kind undeclared and let ingest infer it.

warnings.message: column "{id}" is declared non-nullable but received null; storing a filler value
warnings.meaning: A non-nullable column has no presence bitmap, so there is nowhere to record that a value is absent. The null is stored as a filler — `NaN` for a float column, zero or an empty string elsewhere — and reads back as that filler, not as null. Sorting, filtering and totals all see the filler.
warnings.fix: Declare the column nullable, or clean the data so the value is always present.

warnings.message: set() on unknown column "{colId}"
warnings.meaning: A write named a column the store does not hold, so nothing was written. The row is unchanged and no error is raised.
warnings.fix: Check the column id. A column that is computed rather than stored is not in the store and cannot be written to directly.

warnings.message: column "{id}" is typed {type}, for which the total "{fn}" is not meaningful. Meaningful: {list}. Ignored.
warnings.meaning: A total was set that the column's type cannot support — a sum of dates, an average of text. The total is refused rather than computed, because a number that is arithmetically valid and semantically meaningless is worse than no number at all. The message lists the reductions the type does support.
warnings.fix: Use one of the reductions listed in the message, or change the column's type if the type is what is wrong.

warnings.message: unknown total function "{fn}"; register it in config.totalFns
warnings.meaning: A total, group footer or aggregation named a reduction that is neither built in nor registered. The reduction returns `null`, so the total renders empty rather than showing a wrong number.
warnings.fix: Use a built-in reduction, or register yours in `config.totalFns`.

warnings.message: tree.parentKey produced a cycle; the affected rows were attached to the root.
warnings.meaning: Following `parentKey` from some rows never reaches a root: they point at each other, directly or round a longer loop. Those rows cannot be placed in the tree, so they are shown at the root (or under the named orphan group, when the source is configured with one) rather than dropped. One cycle promotes exactly one row, so a loop of ten does not produce ten copies.
warnings.fix: Break the cycle in the data. A row whose `parentKey` is its own key is the commonest form.

warnings.message: grouping is active on a grid configured with `tree`; the grouping wins and the hierarchy is not shown.
warnings.meaning: A tree and a grouping are two different hierarchies over the same rows and only one can be drawn. The grouping wins, so the tree structure is not shown until the grouping is cleared.
warnings.fix: Clear the grouping (`grid.columns.group([])`) to see the tree again, or accept the grouping.

warnings.message: tree.loadChildren failed for "{key}": {error}
warnings.meaning: A lazily-loaded tree branch failed to load. The branch is deliberately *not* marked as loaded, so collapsing and re-opening it retries — a failure the user can recover from is better than a branch that is permanently empty. A `tree:loadFailed` event is emitted alongside this line.
warnings.fix: The error's message is quoted in the line, and the event carries the error object for your own retry or reporting.

warnings.message: two rows share a tree.path; the later ones were nested beneath the first.
warnings.meaning: Two data rows resolve to the same path, and a path identifies one node. The second and later rows become children of the first, which is the only reading that loses no data — but it invents a level of hierarchy that is not in your data.
warnings.fix: Make each row's path unique, usually by appending the row's own id as the last segment.

warnings.message: tree.path returned an empty path; the affected rows were placed at the root.
warnings.meaning: A row's path is an empty array (or not an array at all), so there is no branch to put it under. It is placed at the root rather than dropped, so the data is still visible.
warnings.fix: Return at least one segment per row. A row that genuinely belongs at the top level should still name itself.

warnings.message: tree.path threw; the affected rows were dropped from the hierarchy.
warnings.meaning: The `tree.path` function threw for a row, so the grid has no place to put it and it is left out of the tree entirely — it is not at the root, it is simply not there.
warnings.fix: The error is attached to the console line. `path` must return an array for every row.

warnings.message: tree is configured with neither `path` nor `parentKey`; rows stay flat.
warnings.meaning: A `tree` block has to say how the hierarchy is derived — a path per row, or a parent key per row. With neither there is nothing to build, so the rows render flat. Silently rendering a flat list is how a misconfiguration goes unnoticed for a week.
warnings.fix: Supply `tree.path` (a function returning the ancestry as an array) or `tree.parentKey`.

warnings.message: unknown data type "{type}"; falling back to "text"
warnings.meaning: The column declared a type that is not registered, so it is treated as `text`: lexical sorting, text filters, no type-driven formatting or editor. Only a type the caller actually wrote is reported — an inference that lands on `text` is a separate, informational line.
warnings.fix: Use one of the built-in types, or register your own type before creating the grid.

warnings.message: computed column "{colId}" read undeclared dependency "{field}". Add it to `value.deps` or the value will go stale.
warnings.meaning: The dependency proxy caught a computed column reading a field it did not declare. The value is computed correctly *this* time; the problem is invalidation — when that field changes, the grid does not know this column depends on it, so the cell keeps its old value and the grid shows a number that is quietly out of date.
warnings.fix: Add the named field to `value.deps`.

warnings.message: unknown compound unit "{symbol}" in system "{system}"; ignoring it
warnings.meaning: A compound rendering lists the units a value is broken across, largest first (`1h 5m 3s`), and one of the symbols is not in the system. That symbol is dropped from the list and the value is rendered across the units that remain, so a component of the value is folded into the next unit down.
warnings.fix: Use symbols the system defines; the rest of the list is unaffected.

warnings.message: unknown display unit "{symbol}"; rendering in {base}
warnings.meaning: The unit a column was told to display in is not in its system — checked both exactly and case-insensitively — so the value is rendered in the system's base unit instead. The stored numbers are unchanged; what the reader sees is a different unit from the one configured.
warnings.fix: Use a symbol from the column's own unit system.

warnings.message: unknown unit system "{system}"; known systems are {list}
warnings.meaning: A unit column named a measurement system that is not registered, so no unit index could be built. The column has no units at all: values render as plain numbers and no conversion happens.
warnings.fix: Use one of the systems listed in the message.
warnings.snippet: columns: [{ id: 'size', type: 'unit', unit: { system: 'data', unit: 'B' } }]

warnings.message: unknown unit "{unit}" in system "{system}"; falling back to {base}
warnings.meaning: The system exists and the base unit named in it does not. The column falls back to that system's base unit, so the numbers are interpreted in a different unit from the one you declared — the values themselves are unchanged, their meaning is not.
warnings.fix: Use a symbol the system defines. The message names the unit it fell back to.

warnings.message: saved views could not be read: {error}
warnings.meaning: The views storage adapter threw on read, so the grid starts with no saved views. Nothing is lost — the stored data is untouched — and the list simply appears empty until a read succeeds.
warnings.fix: The storage error's message is quoted in the line.

warnings.message: saved views could not be persisted: {error}
warnings.meaning: The views storage adapter threw on write. The change is still applied in memory and the change event still fires, so the UI shows the new view; it is gone on the next reload.
warnings.fix: The storage error's message is quoted in the line. A full localStorage quota is the usual cause.

warnings.message: router.query(adapter) needs an adapter with an execute(query) function (a DFQL/DuckDB adapter or a pushdown source); nothing was fetched.
warnings.meaning: `router.query()` pushes a query down to an adapter and fans the result through the ordinary route machinery. The object passed has no `execute`, so there was nothing to call: the promise resolves with the router unchanged and no rows were fetched.
warnings.fix: Pass a pushdown adapter — the DFQL or DuckDB adapter, or your own object with `execute(query, request)` and optional `capabilities`.

warnings.message: attach/subscribe target has no rows.apply and is not a function; its slice goes nowhere. Pass a grid or a handler(change) function.
warnings.meaning: A route was attached to something the router cannot deliver to. Every target is either a viewer with `rows.apply` (a grid, a board, a KPI panel) or a plain `(change) => {}` handler; anything else gets a sink that discards, so the route runs, the metrics count it, and the rows arrive nowhere.
warnings.fix: Pass the viewer itself, or a function that takes the change object.

warnings.message: router.broadcast({ channel }) needs a string channel name; nothing was mirrored.
warnings.meaning: `broadcast()` was called without a channel name, so there is nothing to name the channel after and no channel was opened. Any channel already open is left as it is.
warnings.fix: Pass a channel name that every tab of your application agrees on.

warnings.message: buffer() called with no window or max; applying a default cap of {n} deltas so the buffer stays bounded. Pass { window } or { max } to size it.
warnings.meaning: `buffer()` was called with neither bound. An unbounded buffer on a live feed grows until the tab runs out of memory, so the router applied a default cap rather than doing what was literally asked. Recording is on, with that cap.
warnings.fix: Size the buffer deliberately: `{ window }` in milliseconds for a time span, `{ max }` for a count. Pass `{ max: null }` explicitly if you really mean unbounded.

warnings.message: router.mountDevtools(el) needs a router with metrics()/on() and a DOM element to render into; the panel was not mounted.
warnings.meaning: The observability panel had either no usable router or no element to draw into. A no-op controller is returned — its `destroy()` and `refresh()` do nothing — so calling code is safe, but there is no panel.
warnings.fix: Pass the router and a real element. In a headless environment the panel cannot be mounted at all.

warnings.message: addSource("{id}") was already registered; returning the existing source handle. Use a distinct id per feed.
warnings.meaning: Two feeds were registered under one id. The second call did not create a second source: it returned the handle of the first, so both callers are now pushing into the same stream and the options of the second registration were ignored entirely.
warnings.fix: Give each feed its own id, or keep the handle from the first `addSource` instead of calling it again.
warnings.snippet:
const trades = router.addSource('trades');
const quotes = router.addSource('quotes');

warnings.message: join.missing "{value}" is not hold|passthrough|null; using "passthrough".
warnings.meaning: `missing` decides what happens to a row whose lookup has not arrived: hold it back until it does, let it through unenriched, or let it through with nulls. The value given is none of the three, so the default `passthrough` was used — rows are delivered unenriched rather than being held.
warnings.fix: Use `'hold'`, `'passthrough'` or `'null'`.

warnings.message: join has no `fields`/`select`; rows pass through unenriched.
warnings.meaning: The join resolves — it has a source and both keys — but names nothing to copy across, so the matched lookup row contributes no columns. The rows arrive exactly as they would with no join at all, at the cost of the lookup.
warnings.fix: Name the fields to copy: an array of names, an object mapping source name to destination name, or a function returning the extra properties.

warnings.message: join with a fn `localKey` needs an explicit string/fn `foreignKey`; ignoring the join.
warnings.meaning: When `localKey` is a field *name*, the router uses the same name on the lookup side by default. When it is a function there is no name to reuse, so the lookup side has to be named explicitly; it was not, and the join was dropped.
warnings.fix: Add `foreignKey` — a field name on the lookup rows, or a function that reads one.
warnings.snippet: join: { from: 'customers', localKey: (r) => r.cust.id, foreignKey: 'id', fields: ['name'] }

warnings.message: join needs a `from` (the lookup source id); ignoring the join.
warnings.meaning: A join spec named no lookup source, so the router cannot know what to enrich from. The join is dropped and the route degrades to plain fan-in: rows arrive unenriched rather than the router throwing.
warnings.fix: Set `from` to the id of the source holding the lookup rows.

warnings.message: join needs a `localKey` (a field name or fn); ignoring the join.
warnings.meaning: The join has a `from` but nothing to match on from the left side, so no row can be paired with a lookup row. The join is dropped and rows pass through unenriched.
warnings.fix: Set `localKey` (or its alias `on`) to the field name on the incoming row, or a function that reads it.

warnings.message: relate({ mutual: true }) with a function relation cannot be inverted; the same predicate is applied in both directions. Use a { from, to } key map for a mutual edge.
warnings.meaning: A mutual relation is built by inverting the relation for the reverse direction. A `{ from, to }` key map inverts exactly; a function cannot be inverted safely, so the same predicate is reused in both directions — which is right only if the predicate happens to be symmetric.
warnings.fix: Express a mutual relation as a key map. Keep the function and declare the two directions separately if the relation is genuinely asymmetric.
warnings.snippet: router.relate(a, b, { from: 'id', to: 'parentId' }, { mutual: true });

warnings.message: router.broadcast() needs the BroadcastChannel API, which this runtime does not provide; cross-tab mirroring is off.
warnings.meaning: Cross-tab mirroring uses `BroadcastChannel`, and this runtime has none. No channel was opened; the router behaves exactly as a router that never called `broadcast()`, so other tabs will not see this one's deltas.
warnings.fix: Nothing, in a runtime without the API. In a browser that has it, check that the call is not running in a worker or a context where the global has been removed.

warnings.message: {method}() needs a buffered window; call router.buffer({ window, max }) first to record one.
warnings.meaning: A time-travel method was called on a router that is not recording. Nothing is buffered, so there is no history to seek into, and the call did nothing. Buffering is opt-in because it is the only feature that makes the router hold on to deltas.
warnings.fix: Call `router.buffer()` — with a `window` (milliseconds) or a `max` (number of deltas) — before using the time-travel API.

warnings.message: router.persist() found no usable IndexedDB (a non-browser runtime, private mode, or blocked storage); the router runs in-memory with no durable resume. Pass { storage } to use another backend.
warnings.meaning: Persistence was asked for and no IndexedDB could be opened — a non-browser runtime, a private window, or storage blocked by policy. The router keeps working entirely in memory: nothing is saved, and a reload starts from scratch instead of resuming.
warnings.fix: Supply your own `storage` object with `get`/`set` (localStorage, a server round-trip, anything), or accept the in-memory behaviour.

warnings.message: a route attached with { writable: true } has no onWrite handler (per-route or router-global); the edit was left in place but not persisted. Pass onWrite to route the write.
warnings.meaning: A writable route took an edit and had nowhere to send it. The edit stays visible in the grid — it is not reverted — but nothing was persisted, so a reload loses it. This is the one write path that leaves the screen ahead of the truth, which is why it is reported.
warnings.fix: Give the route (or the router) an `onWrite` handler that sends the change to your backend.
warnings.snippet: router.attach(grid, { writable: true, onWrite: (c) => api.patch(c.key, { [c.colId]: c.value }) });

warnings.message: Data Router: value {value} already routes to another viewer; with overlap:false only the first receives rows. Pass createDataRouter({ overlap: true }) to fan one value to several viewers.
warnings.meaning: Two value-routes claim the same partition value, and the router is in its default exclusive mode, so only the first route receives those rows — the second is attached, live and empty. The check is deliberately strict: it fires only when the value is a scalar and an existing route claims exactly the same one, so distinct-value routing and `overlap: true` are never accused.
warnings.fix: Route each value once, or create the router with `overlap: true` when one value really is meant to feed several viewers.

warnings.message: an edit on a derived (rollup/transform) route is read-only and was reverted; a derived row cannot be inverted to a source row. Make the source route writable instead.
warnings.meaning: A cell was edited in a grid fed by a derived route — a rollup or a transform. The router cannot invert a derived row back to the source rows it came from, so there is nothing to write; the edit was reverted in the grid so that the screen keeps telling the truth.
warnings.fix: Attach the *source* route as writable and edit there, letting the derived view recompute from it.

warnings.message: route "{name}" asked its target to remove {n} row(s) the target does not have (for example "{id}"). The rows are still on screen. This is a key mismatch: the key the route derives for a row is not the key the grid derives for it. Check that the route's `rowKey` names the same value as the grid's.
warnings.meaning: The target reported back that it could not apply some removals because it holds no rows under those keys. The router is the only component that can see both sides, so it says so: the rows the route meant to remove are still on screen and will stay there. It is always a key mismatch — the route and the viewer are deriving different keys for the same row.
warnings.fix: Make the route's `rowKey` produce the same value as the grid's `rowKey`. A numeric id on one side and its string form on the other is the usual cause.
warnings.snippet: router.attach(grid, { rowKey: (row) => String(row.id) });   // and the grid the same

warnings.message: attach({ writable: true }) needs a grid exposing grid.on and grid.edit.setCells; write-back is off for this route.
warnings.meaning: Write-back listens to the target's committed `cell:changed` events through its public event surface, and this target has neither `on` nor `edit.setCells` — it is not an editable grid. The route is attached and delivers rows normally; it simply never sends anything back.
warnings.fix: Attach a grid for a writable route. A plain handler function cannot be written back through, because there is no editing surface to listen to.

warnings.message: dhtmlx-compat does not translate the {kind} key '{key}', so it has no effect. Nothing was applied for it.
warnings.meaning: A configuration or column key from your dhtmlx grid has no counterpart in the compatibility shim, so it was dropped. `{kind}` is `config` or `column`, and `{key}` is the key as you wrote it. A migration that silently ignores half of a column definition is the failure this line exists to prevent: the shim translates what it knows and names everything it does not, once per key rather than once per column.
warnings.fix: Look the key up in the dhtmlx compatibility section of the reference. Where Lattice has an equivalent it is spelled differently and belongs in the native configuration; where it has none, remove the key so the intent is not lost in your source.

warnings.message: dhtmlx-compat does not recognise editorType '{editorType}'; the default text editor was used instead.
warnings.meaning: A column carried a dhtmlx `editorType` the shim has no mapping for. The column is still editable — editing was not switched off — but it was given the plain text editor, so a date, a select or a checkbox column will edit as free text and will accept values its type would have rejected.
warnings.fix: Set the Lattice editor for that column directly (`edit: { editor: 'date' }` and so on), which also gives you the editor options the dhtmlx name cannot carry.
warnings.snippet: columns: [{ id: 'due', type: 'date', edit: { enabled: true, editor: 'date' } }]

warnings.message: dhtmlx-compat collapsed a {n}-row header to its first row. Lattice titles are a single string; the remaining rows were not applied.
warnings.meaning: dhtmlx carries a multi-row header as an array on the column; a Lattice column's `title` is one string. The shim keeps the first row's text and drops the rest, so a second header row that carried a filter box or a sub-heading is gone from the rendered header.
warnings.fix: Model the extra level as a column group, which is how Lattice draws banded headings, and leave `title` as the leaf's own text.
warnings.snippet: columns: [{ id: 'q1', title: 'Q1', group: 'Revenue' }, { id: 'q2', title: 'Q2', group: 'Revenue' }]

warnings.message: dhtmlx-compat does not translate the span key '{key}', so it has no effect. Lattice spans carry only geometry (rowspan/colspan); the cell's value, css and tooltip come from its own column, not the span.
warnings.meaning: `addSpan()` was called with a key beyond the four the shim understands (`row`, `column`, `rowspan`, `colspan`). In dhtmlx a span can also carry the merged cell's text, CSS and tooltip; in Lattice a span is geometry only and the merged cell renders through the column it belongs to, so those keys had nowhere to go.
warnings.fix: Set the appearance on the column instead — its `cell.render`, its `cell.class`, its `tooltip` — and keep the span for geometry.

warnings.message: annotate.add ignored a mark: it needs a known `type` ({types}) and at least two finite {x, y} points in content coordinates.
warnings.meaning: A host-added annotation mark could not be built from its descriptor, so nothing was added to the layer and the call returns the mark count unchanged. Either the `type` is not one the layer draws, or the `points` array has fewer than two usable points — a point with a `NaN`, a string coordinate or a missing axis does not count.
warnings.fix: Use one of the listed types and give at least two points in content coordinates (the same space the grid scrolls in, not screen pixels).
warnings.snippet: grid.annotate.add({ type: 'line', points: [{ x: 10, y: 20 }, { x: 240, y: 90 }] });

warnings.message: autoHeight is off above {n} rows; use autoHeight: 'visible' to measure only rendered rows
warnings.meaning: `autoHeight` measures every row to find its height, which cannot be done for an arbitrarily large row count without measuring the whole dataset. Above the limit the grid degrades to fixed heights, so rows that would have grown to fit their content are clipped instead.
warnings.fix: Use `autoHeight: 'visible'`, which measures only the rendered rows and keeps working at any row count.

warnings.message:
config.board is on but the grid has no columns and no template, so a card would draw nothing. Supply board: { template: '
{{cell.name}}
' } or add columns.
warnings.meaning: As with the gallery and the record card: the board presentation has no template and no columns to build one from, so it is refused and the grid stays a table.
warnings.fix: Give `board` a template, or declare the grid's columns.

warnings.message: Column '{colId}' cell must be an object or a renderer name.
warnings.meaning: The column's `cell` property is neither a renderer name nor a spec object, so the whole cell specification is discarded and the column renders with defaults — no renderer, no template, no decoration, no class rules.
warnings.fix: Give `cell` a renderer name, or an object holding `render`, `template`, `decoration`, `class`, `classWhen` and so on.

warnings.message: column "{colId}" has no editor.
warnings.meaning: An edit was started on a column that resolves to no editor at all — editing is disabled for it, or its type and configuration name nothing that can be built. No editing session started and the cell is unchanged.
warnings.fix: Enable editing on the column and give it an editor, or a type that supplies a default one.

warnings.message: cannot edit a row that is not rendered; scroll to it first.
warnings.meaning: `edit.start()` named a row that is outside the rendered window, so there is no cell element to put an editor into and no editing session was started. The grid renders only the rows in view, so a key that is valid in the data may still have no element.
warnings.fix: Scroll the row into view first and start the edit afterwards.

warnings.message: Column '{colId}' cell.class threw.
warnings.meaning: The `cell.class` function threw while computing a cell's classes. The throw is caught, no extra classes are added for that cell, and the static classes are still applied — so the grid paints and the cell simply misses its dynamic styling.
warnings.fix: The error is attached to the console line. As with a renderer, the function is called for every visible cell including `null` values.

warnings.message: Column '{colId}' classWhen['{class}'] threw.
warnings.meaning: A `classWhen` predicate threw, which is treated as "does not apply": the class is not added to that cell and painting continues. Reported once per column and class, so one broken predicate is one line.
warnings.fix: The error is attached to the console line. The predicate must return `true` to apply the class; anything else, including a throw, means it does not.

warnings.message: Column '{colId}' classWhen['{class}'] must be a function or a rule string.
